speechtext:
That the fifth report of the Joint Committee on Printing of Parliament be concurred in.
He said : The recommendations of the committee are of such importance that before this motion passes, I think I should call attention to them. The committee have spent a good deal of time in examining into the state of affairs in connection with the translation, printing and distribution of French documents. As everybody understands, this is a dual language parliament, that is to say, a parliament in which both languages are upon the same footing. For years past we have had complaints-and very reasonable complaints-of the vexatious, unreasonable delays in the printing and distribution of French parliamentary returns and reports. The committee deemed the matter of sufficient importance to make some investigation, in order to ascertain whether some reform could not be brought about which would result in the adoption of a system more creditable to this House and more satisfactory to the people.
The committee have made three recommendations. The first is to the effect that the ministers should try and get their reports out as soon as possible after the close

of the fiscal year. The present practice seems to be to delay the preparation of these reports in English until within a very few weeks before the opening of parliament. The manuscript of a very large number of these reports consequently goes to the Printing Bureau almost at the end of the calendar year, and sometimes at the beginning of the next calendar year, or six or seven months after the close of the fiscal year. The result is that the King's Printer puts the whole force of the Bureau on the printing of these documents and returns, and is able to turn them out in time for us to have them at the beginning of the session. But the defect of this system in respect of the translation, printing and distribution of the documents in French is this, that all these returns are then turned over to the translators, so that almost a year's work is put upon the translators at once, and it is utterly impossible for them to have these documents ready in reasonable time. The committee suggests that the ministers should endeavour to hurry up the preparation of their reports so as to have them ready as soon as possible after the close of the fiscal year. In the same connection, the committee have thought that some expedition might be obtained in the larger departments if each of these departments had its own special translator in the department itself, who would be handed the English manuscript copy and go on translating at once. In this way the French and English manuscript could be sent at the same time to the Printing Bureau. If that system were adopted and carried out reasonably well, the great majority of the French reports might be laid on the table at the opening of parliament just as the English reports now are.
This is a matter of principle and right, which warrants us in pressing on the House the necessity of bringing about the reform I have indicated. But I do not wish to dogmatize as to the particular way the reform should be accomplished so long as it is accomplished.
These suggestions would not be complete without some reference to the Printing Bureau. The volume of work has grown immensely within the last two years, and so rapidly that it has outrun the facilities of the bureau and rendered it necessary to provide some additions and greater facilities-
And more machinery.

And more machinery should be provided. But with regard to the latter point, the chief trouble is this, that owing to lack of room it is impossible to add any plant. i have visited the Bureau myself several times this session, and while I do not pretend to be more practical than anybody else. I find that the Bureau is too small and crowded in many departments, and is doing its work at great disadvantage.

Take the bindery : a good deal of the delay of which we are complaining arises from the fact that the bindery is largely incapable, owing to want of room, of handling the amount of matter that passes through it. To give an idea of the amount of work done, let me point out that in the month of March the Bureau turned out over $100,000 worth of printing in connection with parliamentary reports.
Another thing which has helped to congest the Printing Bureau is this. They keep the type of all the voters' lists of Canada standing ; and as a result there are 108 tons of type stored away in nooks and corners, which is very difficult indeed to get at when required. But if the Bureau were enlarged and put in proper shape, that would help very much not only in the distribution of the French documents, but in the handling of the copy generally, judiciously and economically. In this way, the small expense that would be incurred in getting the Bureau on a good working basis would in the end save us a great deal of money.
Have you any idea of the cost ?

I am not a practical builder myself, but I fancy that the addition we would require-and we might as well build for twenty or twenty-five years to come-would cost $100,000, but that I do not consider of any great importance if we can get a proper kind of establishment. In 1894 it was felt that the Printing Bureau, was not quite equal to the work it had to do. and the then government had plans prepared for an extension. Of course, w7e can understand why at that time the plan was not gone on with, and since the present government has taken office, no doubt ministers have been so busy that this matter has escaped their attention.
No, I have thought of it many times myself.

I hope that as a result of our recommendations, some reasonable endeavour will be made to bring about the reforms I have indicated. As for myself, I do not care so much how these things are done provided they are done, though it has seemed to me, from the cursory investigation I have been able to make during a few weeks of this session, that these recommendations substantially lay the groundwork on which we can carry out the reform desired. I have no doubt that the reform is indeed a most urgent one. It seems to me a shame that in a parliament of this kind documents in French-which our French Canadian compatriots are as much entitled to have on time as -we are to have the English reports-should be all the way from six months to one year, and even two years, behind the publication of the latter.

(Translation.) In corroboration of the remarks just

offered by tlie bon. member for Shefford (Hr. Parmelee) in moving that the report of the Joint Committee on Printing of Parliament be concurred in, I may say that, as a matter of fact, there seems to exist a deplorable state of affairs in connection with the publication of the French reports. Allow me. Sir, in support of the complaint I have just made, to call your attention to a case of delay incident to the publication of a French report, which has occurred during this very session. I speak from experience when I state that, at the opening of the session the report of the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization, brought down last session, had not yet been printed. It seems to me a shame that in a dual language parliament, that is to say, a parliament in which both languages are upon the same footing, documents of this kind which our French-speaking compatriots are as much entitled to have on time as the English speaking ratepayers are to have the English reports, should be one year behind the publication of the latter.
Having made up my mind to trace the evil back to its source, 1 made inquiries and tried my best to find out who was responsible for that state of affairs. With this end in view, I wrote to the King's Printer, inquiring as to the cause of the vexatious and unreasonable delay in the printing and distribution of that French report. The King's Printer replied to my letter on the 7th of March, and in his communication he gives the date of the receipt of the several portions of said report at the Printing Bureau. The last portion of the copy, tnirty pages in all, was received at the Printing Bureau on the 16th of December, 1900. and as there were still left a few pages, the work could not be completed.
Such were the facts which I brought to the notice of the Joint Committee on the Printing of Parliament. Now, the members of that committee took up the matter, and on the 16th of March I received from Mr. Polkinghorne. clerk of the Printing Committee. a letter which reads as follows :-
Ottawa, Ont., March 16, 1901.
J. H. Legris, Esq., M.P.,
Chairman of Committee on Agriculture.
Dear Sir,-I am instructed by the Joint Committee on the Printing of Parliament to notify you that due inquiry was made with reference to your communication regarding the delay in the printing of the French version of the Report on Agriculture, and that owing to the non-receipt of the copy by the translator. Mr. Genand, from Mr. P. M. Draper, of the Printing Bureau, who had said copy in charge, he was unable to proceed with the translation of the last sixteen pages of the index ; the matter has, however, now been remedied and the work completed, the translation and all copy placed in the hands of the King's Printer and will no doubt be soon distributed.	Yours truly,
(Signed) JOHN A. POLKINGHORNE, Clerk of Printing Committee.
As will be seen from the above letter, from the 16th of December, 1900. to the 10th of March, 1901, Mr. P. M. Draper, of the Printing Bureau, who had the copy in charge, did not deliver it to the French translator, and so Mr. Draper seems to be responsible for the delay in the printing of the French version of that report.
Now, Sir, it seems to me that the employees of the Printing Bureau should be under the control of somebody, and when they are remiss in their duty they should be held responsible for such conduct.
In this case the responsibility for the vexatious and unreasonable delay incident to the publication of that French report seems to fall upon the shoulders of Mr. Draper. Why, Sir, it was but a short time ago that the French version of the report of the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization brought down last session, was distributed. This is a report, Sir, which always proves very interesting to our French Canadian fellow-countrymen, and as I said, they are as much entitled to have that report on time as the English-speaking people are to have the English report, and it is simply intolerable that such a report should be six months or a year behind time in being printed in the French language.
For my part, I believe that apart from the recommendations presented by the Joint Committee on the Printing of Parliament, there should be some other way of remedying that state of affairs, and whenever it is shown beyond doubt that any employee of the Printing Bureau neglects his duty, he should be called to order.
The suggestion of my hon. friend from Shefford (Mr. Parmelee) seems both practical and practicable, and I suppose the House will have no objection to adopting the report.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext:
As a member of the Printing Committee, I can corroborate everything that has been said toy the chairman of that committee. At almost every meeting of the committee since the beginning of the session, we have had complaints regarding the delay in the printing of the French reports. As has been said by the hon. member for Maskinonge (Mr. Legris), the report on Agriculture and Colonization was not published until nearly a year after it had been issued in English. As the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Parmelee) has very well said, the French population are entitled to receive these reports as soon as possible after they are published in English. I believe that some progress has already been made, and much more progress could be made if the present recommendations were carried out. I understand that in the past it has been customary to farm out this translation to a number of people, many of whom were quite incompetent to do the work. Translation is a harder work than people generally believe. It takes a man well versed in both languages to be able to make a proper translation. I am informed that the present staff of translators is a com-

petent staff, and that it is in the interest of a good translation that the work should he limited to these men ; no more translation should he given out. It is the rule, so far as I can gather, that no man is employed to translate any parliamentary work until he has undergone an examination and proved himself capable to do the work that is to be assigned to him. The advantage of keeping these translators together, as they are at the present time, under the control of Hr. Cour-solles and the Speaker of this House, lies in the fact that they can help each other. If you separated them and put one into each department, they would work apart, and in many instances would not have the advantage of being able to confer with each other. If the report presented by the committee is adopted, you would have these men scattered all over the different departments. I would suggest that another method be adopted. When a man has translated the report of one department, he has gone to a great deal of trouble to acquire a knowledge of the technical expressions which are used in the various departments. If yon place that report the following year in the hands of another translator, he will have to go over all the same ground and consult a large number of technical dictionaries, and the work will not be as well done probably as it had been done previously by the man who had already acquired the necessary experience. Therefore, I beg leave to move this amendment, which I hope will be acceptable to the members of the Printing Committee, as an amendment to section 3 :
That the report of each department should be as much as possible translated by the same translator, whose duty it should he to translate from the English copy as fast as it is prepared, so that the French and English copies might go to the Printing Bureau concurrently ; and that the report as amended he concurred in.

I have no hostility to that amendment, but I desire to say a few words upon the report generally of the Printing Committee. One of the chief questions that has been before the committee this session has been the delay incident to the publication of the French report. Every one must admit that the use of the dual language calls for the issuing of the reports concurrently, if possible. But, unfortunately, that has not been possible under existing circumstances. I agree entirely with the amendment that is proposed ; but there is a clause in the report to which I think special attention should be called, that is. the necessity of increased accommodation in the Printing Bureau. I do not know how many members of the House have visited the Printing Bureau, but I think it would be in their own interest, and would enlarge their information, if they would visit the Printing Bureau and find out the conditions that exist there. I notice by the report of the King's Printer, year after year, that the present building has been found altogether inadequate for the requirements of Mr. MARCIL.
the work that is called for. In his report for 1898 he says :
The present building was designed to accommodate the business of the government as it existed in 1886. No reserve of space was provided to meet the increasing demands of a growing country. The building was filled immediately after its erection. In the meantime the country has grown. The business of the departments has greatly increased, but the facilities provided at the Printing Bureau remain unchanged in some essential particulars. The space occupied is the same ; the power of output of the press-room is the same.
The question has been asked here several times during this session, in reference to the printing of several reports, and the information has been given to the House that certain reports had to be printed outside the Bureau. The reason for that subsequently given has been that the Bureau is so crowded at the present time that it is impossible to put on any more hands ; consequently, when the reports are required with some speed and in proper time, they have to be given out in order to have them done when required. I notice, also, that the King's Printer, in his report for the current year, calls attention to the same difficulty :
The year past has been one of constant pressure at the Government Printing Bureau. Keeping pace with the rapid growth of the country and the expansion of its interests, the operations of the government are extending over wider areas and in new directions. Of necessity it follows, therefore, that there must be larger requirements upon the Bureau and a continually
increasing strain upon its resources	The
Government Printing Bureau has been for years occupied to its utmost capacity. There is not room for additional hands. More hands would, in fact, produce less work because the men would be in each other's way. There has been no serious suspension of work-people in any branch since the year 1896, and the work is now beginning to overflow into outside offices	 The need of increased accommodation has been continually pointed out from the very first year the Bureau was opened. In 1889, the late Queen's Printer reported ' that every part of the building was occupied.'
I notice in subsequent reports that be expresses the same opinion. Now, my object in rising is to direct the attention of the House and the government to the fact that an addition to the Bureau is absolutely necessary, that if the Bureau is to meet the requirements of the House and the country, an addition should be made thereto. The composing room, the bindery, in particular, are so crowded that it is absolutely impossible for the hands that are employed there to work with that facility they would otherwise do if they had more space. It is not for me to suggest what form the addition should take, but it seems to me that there should toe, in addition to an extension of the present building, another building provided for storing certain stock they have at the Bureau at the present time. They are compelled to use an attic for storing certain formes, known technically to the printers, which I think are placed in an unsafe con-

dition, and should a fire occur, there would he no possibility of saving them. I think, therefore, the House should press upon the attention of the government the necessity of providing as speedily as possible for the demands of increased accommodation in connection with the Bureau, because increased accommodation means that the Bureau will meet the requirements of the public better than it does at the present time.

I believe every member of the committee will unite in the recommendations which have been presented by our chairman this morning. If the government desire to have the work of the different departments printed efficiently, expeditiously and economically, it is absolutely necessary that the recommendations of the committee, so far as the enlargement of the building and increased accommodation are concerned, should be carried out immediately. 1 do not think it is a satisfactory method of doing business to send the reports of the different departments elsewhere, here and there, to be printed, when we have a bureau where it is intended all this work should be done. That the equipment is sadly deficient in some respects, from the lack of space, is evident to a casual observer. I have taken the liberty on previous occasions of directing the attention of the ministry to the disgraceful accommodation given to the employees in the Bureau, and I hope, in view of the recommendations which have been ma.de this morning, and in view of the unanimity which characterized the members of the committee, and of those who have taken an interest in the work of the Bureau, that the government will make provision before the House rises for a sum sufficient to give the additional accommodation that is so urgently required. It is a fact that the accommodation in the bindery in connection with the Bureau is simply disgraceful. There is not room for one-half the operatives who are steadily employed there. I hope it will not be necessary to refer to this matter again, and that when the House meets at the next session, it will be found that the recommendations of the committee have been adopted, and that the facilities and accommodation which are so urgently required at the Bureau have been provided, so that there will be no longer any reasonable excuse for delay in bringing down the reports at the opening of the session.

There is another point regarding the arrangements for carrying on the work of the Printing Bureau that is worthy of consideration. During the session of parliament there is a great congestion of work, and there is a necessity for employing a large number of additional hands, which is attended no doubt with a great deal of inconvenience and loss of time in consequence of the lack of space for that work. And when the congestion has been in a large degree overcome during the session, a number of hands have
to be dismissed, causing no doubt a great deal of inconvenience, perhaps even some distress. By the enlargement of the works and the adoption of some systematic arrangement of the business, the earlier commencement for publication of the various reports and returns, the management of the Printing Bureau can so adjust the operation of the work that there will not be this call for a large number of hands and followed by the necessity for dismissing many of them. Any hon. gentleman can see that if from one hundred to two hundred journeymen printers are suddenly thrown on the world to seek situations elsewhere, the result must be, if not actual suffering, at least great inconvenience and loss. I trust that at a future session the government will ask for such appropriations as will place the Printing Bureau on a proper and businesslike footing.

It appears to me, Mr. Speaker, that the report of the committee presented by tne hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Parmelee) is a direct censure upon the government for its failure to perform its duty. The law requires that these documents shall be printed in both languages. It is a matter of the utmost importance that they should he printed promptly, for the value of many of these reports depends upon the timeliness of presentation to the House and the countiy. Take, for instance, the report of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Trade and Navigation Returns. These reports are valuable only to the extent that they give to the people prompt information as to the trade. The business men, importers and manufacturers who are watching the trade of the country require these reports, and they require them promptly. We are told that some reports are a year, a year and a half, or even two vears behind time in being printed in the French language. But many of them are behind time being printed in English. They should not be behind time in either language. When a page of printing has to be done it does not cost any more to do it promptly
It costs less, as a matter of fact.

The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) tells us that it costs less, and I can quite uuderstand why that should be so. There is all the greater reason why the government, if it did its duty could present these documents to the House and the public with due promptitude. I am glad the Printing Committee has presen t ed this report, and I hope that the government will not hereafter, as they have done year after year, seek to evade their responsibility for lack of promptness in presenting these reports by making the excuse that the Printing Bureau is not able to do the work. This is no proper or sufficient excuse at all. The Printing Bureau should be sufficiently well equipped to do the work and do it quickly. And, as we are told,

tliis would mean not a greater expense but an actual saving of money, and it would give us these reports at a time when they have the greatest value, instead of at a time when their value has greatly depreciated or been entirely lost.
Amendment agreed amended agreed to.

speechtext:
1.	Has the attention of the government been called to the fact that an effort is being made by aliens to secure the permission of the municipality of the city of Quebec to erect a monument to the memory of the American General Montgomery who led the American forces in an unsuccessful attempt to capture the city of Quebec V
2.	If so, has the government taken any action in the matter ?
3.	If the permission of the municipality of Quebec has been given for the erection of such monument or memorial, is it the intention of the government to permit its erection or will the government permit its erection ?

A petition has been received by the government from the United Empire Loyalist Association, if I remember right, against the erection of a monument to General Montgomery in the city of Quebec. We have no information yet upon the subject, but if the municipal corporation of Quebec allows the erection of a monument upon its own ground I doubt if the government has power to interfere. I have asked information from the city of Quebec as to what has really been done, but I have not yet received this information. As soon as i get it 1 shall be glad to communicate it to the House. In the meantime, if my private information is correct, the permission which has been sought is not to erect a monument to the memory of General Montgomery, but simply to place a tablet showing the place where he fell. For some thirty years, and perhaps more, there has been' a tablet on the cliff with the inscription :
* Here Montgomery fell.'
As I understand it there is no other intention but to have a similar tablet.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Is that to be erected by the municipal authorities of Quebec ?
I think it was erected by some friends of Montgomery, and I also understand that it was looked after at one time by the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company, but as to that I have no information.

Last season's business. Then, the statement goes on to give details. We shall perhaps have this matter up again. I should like the hon. minister to make a statement as to the government's policy. What was the reason for the failure of the arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway-for I suppose that is the cause of the falling off of the trade, that company not having carried the usual amount for export from Montreal to St. John. speechtext: It is only as to the figures and facts, I want to know whether the facts as stated are correct.

I have not seen what the hon. gentleman refers to, therefore I could not speak as to the accuracy of the statements. I admit that the amount of export business which was done at St. John last winter wa's much less than in previous years ; but as to the difference in the value of the exports or as to the difference in the quantity in any particular, I am unable to state off-hand. I would, therefore, scarcely undertake to pass upon the correctness of the figures which the hon. gentleman has read, nor do I think at the present time it would be desirable for me to go into the question of the difference which arose between the Intercolonial Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway made certain demands upon the Intercolonial Railway, to which I did not deem it reasonable nor in the interest of the Intercolonial Railway to accede, and I declined to entertain their proposals. The result was that the season became so far advanced before the Canadian Pacific Railway Company realized that the government had determined to adhere to the attitude they had taken up, that I apprehend a good deal of business which would otherwise have been taken to St. John was diverted el'sewhere. I have heard myself that the traffic was handed over by the Canadian Pacific Railway to the Grand Trunk Railway. I have always been ready, and am now, to entertain any reasonable proposal for an interchange of traffic with the Canadian Pacific Railway, which I believe would not be injurious to the interest of the Intercolonial Railway ; but I have not felt myself, even though interested in the port of St. John, and anxious to see the busines's of that port grow to the greatest possible extent-I have not felt that it is my duty to subordinate what I believe to be the interest of the Intercolonial Railway, and therefore of the country, to the demands of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I am very anxious that the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Intercolonial Railway should proceed harmoniously together, I am anxious to make traffic arrangements with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I hope to be able to make such arrangements as will be fair and mutually advantageous. But a one-sided agreement I will not enter into with the Canadian Pacific Railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The statement was made in the House the other day that the grades on the Grand Trunk Railway to Portland were 'Such that they could take trains

of fifty or sixty cars more favourably than to St. John. I understood that the Canadian Pacific Railway were willing to make an arrangement with the government to carry a part of their ocean freight to St. John, and to fix the gradients of their road which are unfavourable in comparison with the Grand Trunk Railway. Have they some kind of an arrangement with the government with reference to that trade ? They complain, of course, that the western-bound traffic on the Intercolonial Railway is being diverted from them to the Grand Trunk Railway, that an unfavourable arrangement to the Canadian Pacific Railway was made with the Grand Trunk Railway. I would like to know when the debate comes up again whether any proposition of that kind has been made to the Canadian Pacific Railway for the purpose of carrying possibly the whole of their ocean-bound traffic to St. John. Then I see also that a large portion of grain, perhaps 2,000,000 or 3,000,000 bushels, has been carried over the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal. If I am rightly informed-and the minister will correct me if I am not-that freight which was taken from the Grand Trunk Railway was carried at the rate of 4 cents a bushel from Montreal to St. John. That was American grain taken by the Grand Trunk Railway from Chicago along its Midland service, and taken to St. John at the rate of 4 cents per bu'shel. I have heard that other parties in Montreal, shippers bringing down Manitoba and North-western grain to Montreal, were anxious to enter into similar arrangements for the carrying of grain from Montreal to St. John, and they found it impossible to make an arrangement with the Intercolonial Railway for less than 10 cents per bushel. Parties have told me that they went to your officers in Montreal and tried to make an arrangement, and found that that was the best they could do. The minister, perhaps, will be able to tell whether my information is correct.

Without having had any conference with the officers of the Intercolonial Railway in respect of these matters of which the hon. gentleman speaks, and not having heard of them myself, I do npt hesitate to inform my hon. friend that he has been absolutely misled. In the first place it i's incorrect to say that we took grain from the Grand Trunk Railway last year to St. John. If we have done so. I was not informed of it. I know that our traffic officials in Montreal communicated with the general manager, who communicated with me, and discussed the question of rates, and it was in every instance in respect of freight that was reaching us by the Canada Atlantic Railway. .
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I meant the Canada Atlantic Railway instead of the Grand Trunk Railway.

The hon. gentleman said the Grand Trunk Railway. My impression is that the whole of the grain that was exported from St. John last year came over the Canada Atlantic Railway. I think I can say with confidence that no such proposition as the hon. gentleman speaks of avs having been made by western shippers, was made to the Intercolonial Railway and refused. I do not believe that any demand, in fact I know that no such demand, was made by the Intercolonial authorities, I am confident they made no such discrimination, and were not unwilling to make fair and reasonable terms with other shippers if any freight had been offered. As to that statement, I may say that the hon. gentleman has been misled.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I heard you carried it at 4 cents a bushel.
I think probably that would not be far astray. The price varied through the season somewhat.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I wish to make this assertion. If grain is carried by the Intercolonial as far as Moncton it would be just as easy to ship it at Halifax as to divert it to St. John, and as every one knows the shipping facilities are better at Halifax than at St. John. The Minister of Public Works stated yesterday that the harbour of St. John required certain dredging at the entrance. Well, the harbour at Halifax will never want any dredging.
What about the fogs ?
There is double the quantity of fog at and around the Bay of Fundy that there is about the harbour of Halifax at any time.

If any reflections were cast upon the harbour of St. John, I could have answered them very effectively. While I am not going to say a word-perhaps I could not if I wished to-which would reflect in any degree upon the harbour at Halifax as compared with the harbour of St. John, I do not think that anything true can be said in favour of Halifax, as against St. John, or that St. John will not stand a fair comparison with Halifax. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Ross) says that when grain is brought from Montreal to Moncton it could as well be taken to Halifax as to St. John, l would just call the attention of my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Ross) to the fact that there would be necessarily some difference. You cannot haul a train-load of grain a hundred miles further, up a very heavy grade, without adding something to the expense. I do not say it would be a large proportion, but there would necessarily be some difference between the two.
164}
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Where is that heavy grade ?
The heavy grade, as the hon. gentleman will know, is at Folleigh; heavier and longer than on the Intercolonial Railway at any point, I think.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is there any difference between the ocean rates from St. John as compared with the rates from Halifax ?

I am glad my hon. friend has asked the question, because it affords me an opportunity of replying to it. If the harbour of St. John is not as inviting to steamship companies as any other harbour on that coast, then let the harbour of St. John take the consequence of any inferiority. But, I think it will be found that those engaged in the ocean steamship business will as readily come to the harbour of St. John as to any other harbour upon the coast in British territory. It may be some inducement that they are likely to get at St. John a good deal of business of a kind which does not offer elsewhere. At all events, I think there will be nothing unfavourable said against the harbour of St. John by shipping men.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: So far as I am concerned, coming as I do from the province of Ontario, I have no prejudices in favour of Halifax, St. John, Montreal or Quebec. The question for we farmers is, from which port can we get our grain cheapest to the English market. I do not care whether my grain goes from St. John or Halifax, but I do care which is the cheapest port. If it costs more to haul grain to Halifax, then the question arises : Will the lower ocean freights at Halifax compensate for the more expensive railway haul ?

I do not think there is any difference made by the steamship companies between the ocean rates from St. John and the ocean rates from Halifax. In fact, I believe the same rate prevails from New York as from Boston, from Boston as from Portland, and from Portland as from St. John or Halifax. It is my impression that the same rate prevails at all the Atlantic ports.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Just a word. I have had some experience with steamship captains for fourteen years, and if they were asked to-day whether they would prefer calling at St. John or Halifax, you would get a direct and definite answer that they would prefer coming to Halifax. Once you leave Halifax harbour you are on the wide ocean.
I do not care about that. Is it cheaper from Halifax ?

When you come to the Bay of Fundy, you have intricate sailing to

get into the harbour of St. John. I wish to say in justice to the harbour of St. John, that the feeling in the city of Halifax is, that the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) is not at all too favourable to the harbour or the city of St. John.
Oh.

I am sorry to hear that I am not favourable to the city and port of St. John. Now, as to what the member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) said with regard to the relations between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Intercolonial Railway. The hon. gentleman stated that west-bound business is all virtually transferred from the Intercolonial Railway to the Grand Trunk Railway by virtue of the arrangement made with them. I do not intend to enter into that in my present statement, but, if that is the case it is not the fault of the Intercolonial Railway. The field is open to the Canadian Pacific Railway if it chooses to occupy it. We have over and over again stated to the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway that we are prepared to make arrangements with them to transfer westbound freight to them at Ste. Rosalie or Montreal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is not that part of your contract with the Grand Trunk Railway in return for the terminal facilities at Montreal ?

No, it is not. All that is effected by that contract is the unconsigned freight. It is open to the Canadian Pacific Railway to go into our territory and to solicit freights, even if the whole body of the traffic is to be transferred to them at Ste. Rosalie. We are willing to make arrangements with them, and we had arrangements made between them and our official stall', which arrangements were rescinded, not by ourselves but by the Canadian Pacific Railway. They will not accept freight from us at" Ste. Rosalie. They have insisted that we should deliver it to them at St. John. That is to say, that we should allow them to come into our territory and make arrangements with the shippers to send freight on our line to the nearest point of the connection with them instead of at the end of our line. I 'have stated over and over again in this House, and the hon. gentleman must understand what the nature of the difficulty between the Canadian Pacific Railway and ourselves is. He must understand it, and therefore, I cannot understand why he asks me what the nature of the difficulty is. It must be familiar to him. It is simply a question of a fair exchange of traffic and of an equitable and fair arrangement between the two railway companies. We are prepared to agree to what is fair and reasonable. We do not think they are. We rescinded a cer-Mr. ROSS (Victoria).
tain contract which was entered into a great many years ago, and since the rescinding of that contract we have had no arrangement. I have instructed my officers to discuss the matter with the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway, but owing to the absence of the principal officers of the Canadian Pacific Railway no progress has yet been made. I do not despair that progress will be made. The very instant that they are prepared to offer us fair traffic terms, we are prepared to agree to such fair traffic terms. I have gone so far as to say that I will submit the question as to what under the circumstances would be fair traffic terms to the arbitrament of any disinterested, competent, outside railway man or men, and I am prepared at this moment to do it. I cannot submit to the demand of another railway company upon us, as representing the Intercolonial Railway, and say, that because they make it, therefore, we must concede it. There must be an element of give and take in any kind of contract or bargain. I maintain that I have met everything that has been proposed to us in the spirit of desiring a fair arrangement. I cannot do anything more.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think the sole difficulty in regard to taking freight to St. John, results from the hon. minister not being able to make an arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway. So long as there is an impossibility of carrying out any arrangement with the hon. minister there is no use of sending any ocean-bound freight to St. John. In answer to the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane), the hen. minister endeavoured to lead the committee to believe that the Canadian Pacific Railway have the right to all the west-bound freight on the Intercolonial Railway at the terminals. He forgets that he made an arrangement that all the unconsigned freight will be turned over-
How could I forget it when I stated it a moment ago ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You did not state it.
I beg your pardon. I stated it just before I sat down.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What did you state ?
I said that the arrangement with the Grand Trunk Railway only referred to unconsigned freight. There is not an hon. gentleman in the House but heard me say that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That is what 1 say. That the agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway is only in reference to unconsigned freight, which is ninety-nine one

hundredths of the west-bound freight. The hon. minister knows it; there is no use talking about that. If I am sending material to Chicago I send it directly to the Canadian Pacific Railway. I suppose the Canadian Pacific Railway has its own arrangement by which if its road does not reach Chicago it carries that freight.	Ninety-nine one-hundreths of the freight that is collected by the Intercolonial Railway in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island is unconsigned freight. You are giving, therefore, nearly the whole of the traffic of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, by the agreement which you have made with them in reference to your terminals. Then, the hon. minister expects the Canadian Pacific Railway to make an arrangement to carry all their ocean-bound freight to St. John, when they can get no return freight from St. John to Montreal. That is exactly the position. The hon. minister when he made that arrangement and when he found fault with the monstrous agreement that was made by his predecessors with the Canadian Pacific Railway and thought he was going to do so much better, that he would no longer have any such agreement as that, finds himself in the position that he is in to-day of nearly ruining the port of his native province. He will never be able to get it out of that position until he comes back to the terms of this monstrous agreement which his predecessors had made with the Canadian Pacific Railway. What is the use of talking about that ? The Canadian Pacific Railway have the right to make a canvass from one end of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to the other for the purpose of getting freight. Undoubtedly they have. So has any railway the right to go into any other railway's territory for the purpose of doing that. What the Intercolonial Railway ought to do is to act fairly by the two railways and arrange equally with them for carrying the traffic westward to its destination. But, the hon. minister by the agreement which he made with the Grand Trunk Railway as to the terminals in Montreal, has given an absurd preference to the Grand Trunk Railway by stipulating that the unconsigned freight on the Intercolonial Railway must be delivered at Ste. Rosalie or Montreal to the Grand Trunk Railway.

This is a matter proceeding from the engineering branch of the department, and has not been stimulated, so far as I know, by any political influence. I cannot think that the conditions are as the hon. gentleman states ; I think he must be misinformed. I do not suppose that he professes to speak from personal knowledge. I

have no complaint to make of liis calling my attention to the matter, however, and before the work is authorized I will make further inquiry.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: My information is that this Eel River is simply a village of about 200 population, and that the only industry there is a lumber and shingle factory, carried on by Wm. Currie & Company. X do not know anything about it personally ; but I am informed that the gentleman who represents the county of Restigouche (Mr. Reid) is interested in that industry, and people would naturally think that would account for this expenditure. I am also informed that the lumber is practically all cut in this section, and therefore, whatever need there may have been in the past for increased railway facilities, that need has gone by ; that there is a very good station and freight-house there at the present time ; and that the expenditure is not necessary, and would be much better devoted, for instance, to improving the facilities at Campbellton.

The station at Campbellton is being well looked after : I do not think there is cause for complaint. But Eel River is, I think, considered to have as good an outlook for increased business as any station of that class on the line. It is an outlet for a very large agricultural population and is a settlement of 300 families-so I am informed by the hon. member for Restigouche.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: My information is that the population is less than 200.
Then I shall have to leave that matter between my hon. friend and the representative of the county.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is the hon. member for Restigouche not financially interested in the firm of Wm. Currie & Company ?
I am not connected in any way with the firm of Wm. Currie & Co.
No financial interest ?
No.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I notice, on looking over the proposed agreement submitted to Mr. Clergue to sign, that it is entirely different from that for which the order in council of the 9th October last provides. This agreement is only for 25,000 tons of rails. Has the minister had communication, verbally or otherwise, with Mr. Clergue.
Verbally, I have had.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is Mr. Clergue agreeable to the change of agreement ?
I can hardly 'say that he is, because there is not any change in the proposal. The agreement is exactly what was contemplated and authorized by the order in council.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When the matter was fully discussed in the House on a previous occasion, we found that the agreement which was then submitted to us, and which was based on the order in council, wa's for 125,000 tons of rails, and is entirely different in that respect from the agreement now before us. The former agreement was for the delivery of 25,000 tons within the year and a subsequent yearly delivery of 25,000 tons during four years, making 125.000 tons in all. In the agreement then submitted to us, the hon.-minister said there was an error, and that It had not been approved by him as head of the department, although it wa's strictly in accord with the order in council.
I did not admit that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The present agreement is only for 25,000 tons of rails. Surely Mr. Clergue, who got subscriptions to this company and started the steel industry at Sault Ste. Marie on the faith of a contract for 125,000 tons, must have had some negotiations with the hon. minister before he consented to this change. I wish to know whether any communications, oral or otherwise, were had with Mr. Clergue, as the result of which Mr. Clergue consented to a modification of the contract.

I see that I shall have to repeat all that I have already said in the House, because my previous 'statement has not dvv^elt on the recollection of the hon. gentleman, and he is even now not paying any attention to my reply.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, I am.

I stated then as clearly as I

could, that we had made an explicit arrangement with Mr. Clergue, or the Lake Superior Power Company, to give them a contract for one year for 25,000 tons, and we had an understanding with them that that contract would be continued four succeeding years at the rate of 25,000 tons per year, making in all 125,000 tons. That statement was criticised, but I could not gather whether hon. gentlemen opposite objected to the agreement, or whether they objected that I had not stated the agreement correctly. The order in council was then put in the hands of hon gentlemen opposite, and that entirely bore out my statement as to what our arrangements with the Lake Superior Power Company were.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The order in council seemed to say that it was for 150,000 tons.
I hope the hon. gentleman is large enough to get out of the little technical question that might arise from a typewritten error.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Surely the hon. gentleman will say that it is something more than technical, and that unless it was a clerical error, it meant a good deal.

It has been shown that the copy of the recommendation of the order in council contained a clerical error, because in two places it states four year's, and in one place five years. Unless we do not care to discuss the question on its merits, let us not embarrass it by any reference to clerical mistakes. It was clearly the intention and purpose of the government to make an explicit contract with the Lake Superior Power Company for one year, and that there was an understanding that each subsequent year during four years, we were to make a new agreement for 25,000 tons of rails. The agreement which has been put into the hands of the hon. member for Lanark is entirely in accord with the terms of the order in council and the explanations I have repeatedly given to this House. The preamble read's as follows
Whereas, by an order in council, dated the 9th day ol October, 1900, authority was given, on the recommendation of the sail minister, for the execution of a contract for the purchase from the company, during the year 1901, of 25,000 tons of first quality steel r :ils, of eighty pounds to the yard, manufaccured in Canada, and of such section as might fro n time lo time be approved by the minister, for the sum of $32.60 per ton, delivered (o.i.f.) either at Levis or Montreal, as the minister might specify; and authority was by such order also given the making of a contract with the company. during the four years next succeeding for the purchase of 25,000 tons per annum of steel rails of the same weight of quality, manufactured in Canada, at prices to be governed by the prices in open market in Great Britain, to be settled in each year fcr the year next succeeding.
That Is the nature of this contract, and it is precisely the contract which, I have stated and explained to the House, the government proposed to make. I myself read to Mr. Clergue this very proposed contract, and asked him if be bad any fault to find with it. He bad not a single criticism ; he could not have, because it was expressly agreed with Mr. Clergue long ago, away back in August, that we could only make the contract with him for a year, hut we would give a promise, we would have an understanding, and he was thoroughly satisfied to take our assurance upon the subject. He has been satisfied to take that assurance, and is satisfied now to do so. We have made no contract, but we are under moral obligations, undoubtedly, to the Lake Superior Power Company to make a contract with them year after year ; and we will do it, provided everything is satisfactory. I cannot understand wherein the hon. gentleman discovers any dissimilarity between the contract which we propose to enter into with Mr. Clergue and the order in council. I would like him to show it if he can.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals lias said just what I expected him to say. He admits that the order in council hinds the government in a contract for five years ; that this is the first instalment of it for the delivery of
25,000	tons ; and under the order in council, he feels himself not only morally, hut legally, bound to the conditions of the first-
He did not say that; I followed him very closely.
No, no ; I said it was only a moral obligation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Let me understand the hon. minister ; I will state what I understood him to say, and if I am misiaken, I will withdraw it. I understood him to say that when the first part of the contract for 25,000 tons is performed, be feels himself and the government feel themselves morally hound to enter into an agreement, and he will do it, for the succeeding four years for the delivery of 25,000 tons a year-
Not for four years, hut for year after year.

When Mr. Clergue performs this part of the contract the Minister of Railways feels himself morally bound to carry out the rest of the order in council. Or, in other words, he carries out what he would be compelled legally to do
No, no.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
No, no.

Hon. ill'. HAGGART. Tlie government are bound by their
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: No, they are not.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This is a contract with an individual, and the Individual has signed that contract.
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: However, it matters not. The contract is for 125,000 tons with the Clergue Company, a specific contract for the delivery of 125,000 tons at a certain price, and upon the performance of that, the company to have the right, morally anyway, according to the minister, to the rest of their contract being performed. And the hon. minister says himself that they will do it. Mr. Clergue never raised a company on the strength of having a contract with the government for a contract of 125,000 tons of steel rails, and put the prospectus before his company and declared that he had this contract, only to come back afterwards and say : I am sorry that I was mistaken. No ; he is going to get his pound of flesh ; he is going to have his contract carried out. Now, the hon. minister last year, as I understood him, told us that he was treating with two steel companies for the purpose of furnishing the rails, that he had negotiations, not only with the Clergue Company, but with the steel company in Nova Scotia. Does the hon. minister say that he did not make that statement last year ?

I do not know precisely to what the hon. gentleman refers, but according to my recollection all I could have said was what I stated when the question of the railway subsidies was up. I pointed out to the committee that we included in the subsidy resolutions a clause to the effect that we would require that the rails to be put on these new railways should be of Canadian manufacture, if they could be obtained on fair and reasonable terms. If my memory serves me well, some hon. member asked the question, what probability there was of that, and I stated that not only one, but possibly two companies, or even more, might be prepared to fulfil a contract at that time ; that if the rails could be had in Canada, the clause would do good, and if the rails could not be procured in Canada, it would do no harm.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I can verify my recollection of the hon. minister's statement, because I read the report of it but a few days ago. My recollection is, that he said that he was negotiating with a couple of steel companies who were competing, and who, no doubt, would satisfactorily furnish the government with steel rails.
I think I must ask the hon. gentleman to refer to what I said, for his recollection does not agree with mine.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not know what the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) refers to, but I remember that at the time when the negotiations were going on there was no company in Nova Scotia prepared to make proposals wdth regard to steel rails. We hoped that they would be in such a position shortly.
The Clergue Company is not making them.
They were proposing and offering to make steel rails, but there was no company in Nova Scotia proposing to and offering to make steel rails at the time of these transactions.

The hon. Minister of Finance may be perfectly correct, but I am afraid I must draw his attention to the ipsissima verba of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, who assured the House that he was negotiating with a couple of steel companies for the furnishing of these supplies.

At the time the railway resolutions came before the House, there were people who proposed the establishment of a plant, I think at Midland, to make steel rails. Just who the people were I do not recollect, but I think they hoped to be able to induce the Cramps of the United States to take up the business in Canada. But, it never materialized. I do not think that the hon. gentleman will find that I said that we were negotiating with a company.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: However, that is my remembrance of it. I have sent for the ' Hansard,' and I will be able to verify my statement, if it is correct. But I hunted it Up a couple of days ago, and I think my memory of it was confirmed. I do not intend to discuss the question at present, but my memory of it, I am sure, is correct.
You may be.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am sometimes wrong, but my memory is surely correct in reference to this, that the Minister of Railways and Canals, in his statement to the House, said that he was negotiating with a couple of companies, and he had no doubt he would be able to make contracts for steel rails as cheap in Canada as anywhere else. I was going to ask the minister to produce the correspondence with the different companies with reference to this Clergue affair.
We have no such correspondence.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is unfortunate *when ministers make statements in the House on the strength of verbal communications with companies or individuals. Any statement of that kind should be founded upon written correspondence. If there is no written correspondence of that kind, there should be no reference to it.

In order that there may be no misunderstanding, I do not hesitate to say, for I felt a deep interest in this matter, that at the time of this arrangement with Mr. Clergue there was no company in Nova Scotia making steel rails, or professing to make steel rails. Within a recent period a movement has been started by the Dominion Iron and Steel Company towards making steel rails, and I hope to find it will be successful. But so far as this relates to the Clergue transaction, I have no hesitation in stating that at that time there was no company making rails, professing to make rails, or offering to make rails. Whatever may have occurred subsequently with regard to future transactions, is another matter.

The Minister of Finance surely does not accuse me of making a statement that there were any parties making, proposing or offering to make steel rails in Nova Scotia. I did not say anything -of the kind.
He said something very much like it.

I was referring to the remarks of the Minister of Railways and Canals, in which he stated that he was negotiating with a couple of firms for the purpose of furnishing steel rails, in Canada. I did not say a word about Nova Scotia. I may have incidentally drawn the conclusion that the offer may have come from Nova Scotia.
The hon. gentleman referred to Nova Scotia only three minutes ago.

The Minister of Finance may be perfectly right, I may have drawn the inference that the offer was from Nova Scotia. But I did not accuse the Minister of Railways and Canals of saying anything of the kind: I will accept the explanation of the minister that perhaps it was from Midland, or somewhere else ; but the conclusion I drew at the time was that manufacturers in Nova Scotia were in competition with Mr. Clergue. All the information I have on the subject is the statement of the minister that he was negotiating with a couple of firms for the purpose of furnishing rails.
The hon. gentleman has said that he is very certain that his recollection is correct of what I said.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I will get the ' Hansard.'

That is the better way to settle it, because I have a recollection of exactly what I stated. I could not have stated to this House that we were negotiating with any one to furnish the government with rails except the Clergue Company, or the Lake Superior Company. The Lake Superior Company had sent us in a communication by that time, a copy of which has been placed in the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Possibly the minister is now in a position to inform the House of the probability of the Clergue Company furnishing any rails in the course of the present year. Is he in a position to state whether the Clergue Company is likely to furnish any rails in the course of this year 1 And, furthermore, if in the end it should appear that the Clergue Company will not be able to furnish rails, what arrangements has he in view for supplying the steel rails for the Intercolonial Railway the present year ?

My statement to the House the other day is strengthened and confirmed by what Mr. Clergue himself has said during his recent visit here ; he says he is undoubtedly going to be able to deliver us these rails under this contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Manufactured where ?
Manufactured in Canada.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: At Sault Ste. Marie ?

Manufactured in Canada. That is what he says. If perchance we should not get the rails from him, I have not considered yet in what direction we may look for rails. I will say this, however, and I say it with confidence, and it will be some comment upon the criticism which hon. gentlemen opposite have made, that we cannot go into the market to-day and make a contract for rails for delivery during this present season, at any less price than that stipulated in this contract. That is a fact which the committee can accept from me. I know it for several reasons. I know that the Grand Trunk Railway have been endeavouring to make a contract for
50,000	tons of rails in the United States, and an offer was made to them ten or fifteen *days ago at $28 per ton, at the works at Pittsburg, or whatever place the rails were made. They have got to pay between $5 and $6 a ton to get these rails brought from Pittsburg to Montreal. Therefore, you have got to pay between $32 and $33 a ton for rails to-day, and let any gentleman who wants

to make a contract apply to any manufacturer in the United States, and he will find that he cannot make any better bargain than we have made, for present delivery.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is quite natural. You could not make a contract to-day for rails for present delivery.
For delivery in the autumn, in this season.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Certainly, no one will make a contract now, or in the beginning of June, for rails to be supplied in July, August or September. But when we were discussing the matter the contract could have been made for much less.
I am glad to get that acknowledgment from the bon. gentleman, because not only he, but a dozen members on the other side, pointed to the present price and said we were paying $7 more than we should.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But the minister will find that all the statements were regarding a contract made in October, the prices were then stated on this side of the House, and it was shown that he made the contract for $7 a ton more than rails could be bought for then. You cannot go into the market to-day and buy rails for delivery a month or two months hence ; it would be an absurdity.

I ask the hon. gentleman to turn up what he himself said on that subject in this House, and he will find that the criticism he made upon this transaction was to the effect that you could buy rails in the United States to-day for $26 per ton.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: At the time the contract was made.

At the time the hon. gentleman made the statement he said the price was $26 a ton. He is not willing to go back to a date at the time when this arrangement was made with Mr. Clergue in the month of August. He has to come down to the month of November before he will find the price quoted in the United States below the price I have named. He will find, if he chooses to look at the published reports in the trade papers, what steel rails were quoted for at those dates. To-day, he has to pay $28 a ton, and I do not believe he could get delivery of any part this season. I do not care what portion of the season he chooses. Up to the close of navigation he cannot get a contract for delivery at the works of any of the companies at less than $28 a ton. I do not think he can get it at $28 a ton, because an offer made to the Grand Trunk Railway Company for 50,000 tons at $28 a ton ten days ago was withdrawn because the price is going up.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Two days before I made the statement in this House I had seen a contract made by the Canadian Pacific Railway at $25 a ton for steel rails delivered in Montreal this year.

I have listened to the debates in connection with these steel rails, and I have listened with a great deal of pain to the debates in connection with the Intercolonial Railway, which is under the charge of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. The impression left upon my mind and, I think, upon the minds of the people of this country, is that this is a department which requires a great deal more looking after than it gets from other members of the government. I take the liberty of saying in the face of the country that the way in which that contract was made, the way in which that contract was presented to the House was most unbusinesslike and that the enormous amount of explanation that was required to be made by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals is something that would not be tolerated in a business house. If the manager of a department in any large business, in connection! with the management of his department, made the statement that the hon. minister has made about this contract, about the way in which it was received by Mr. Clergue and the way in which it was understood by him, he would be discharged. It has required an amount of explanation which leaves the matter still unexplained. The hon. gentleman made a statement just now regarding the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Osier). The statement which the hon. member for Centre Toronto made I have clearly in my recollection. That hon. gentleman stated that a day or two before he made that statement the railway company that he is connected with had made a large contract at $25 a ton. It is no use for the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to come down to this House and say that at this particular moment he could not do a particular thing. We are not discussing that matter at the present time. We are discussing the arrangement he made some months ago, an arrangement which was misstated to this House. The statement that the hon. minister made was that he had made an absolute contract for 25,000 tons and no more, but. that there was a kind of understanding, an indefinite understanding that an additional 100,000 tons of rails were to be taken at a different price. I contend that any contractor such as Mr. Clergue is, who would be willing to take a contract of that kind, would be a worse business man than I imagine Mr. Clergue to be. He had to take the order in council to lay before capitalists, and it was no use taking an indefinite contract before such business men in order to interest them in this work. He had to take a definite positive contract founded upon the order in (council, and to say that this is merely a

moral obligation is to go very wide of the facts. In connection with business matters every day people make verbal arrangements which are more than moral contracts. They are contracts that must be carried out. It is an absolute contract that he made with the government of this country and he says he is going to carry it out. Under these circumstances I do not think it is very dignified for a minister of the Crown to be twisting and turning these matters in the way in which he has done. I think if he had come forward when first challenged on this matter and said :	Yes, I made a contract for
the sake of starting a new industry in this country which you hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House dare not challenge, because this is your own policy. If the hon. gentleman had done that he would have been able to get out of his present position with a great deal less difficulty than it takes him now to get out of it. To charge hon. members on this side of the House with making misstatements, I think, comes with very bad grace from him because the statement he made in connection with the first contract for steel rails was an absolute misstatement of the case, a misstatement of the case according to Mr. Clergue's own understanding of it, who, being the party of the second part, might be expected to have some kind of an understanding of the character of the contract he was taking down to Philadelphia or elsewhere to procure funds to get these works in operation. This House, I contend, should be a business House. To this House the people of the country have a right to look for a business example, an example as to what a real contract, or a moral contract, or a legal contract is. I contend that when once the government have pledged themselves by an order in council they are bound in honour to carry it out. Therefore, much harm will be done in the country if this debate should go on in the way in which it has been conducted, and I call upon the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to look into this whole matter carefully and make such a statement as he need not be ashamed of, and such as the country may not be ashamed of. He has received a large amount of assistance from other hon. members of the government. The hon. Minister of Finance has been most active in endeavouring to get the hon. gentleman out of the disagreeable hole in which he has placed himself, and I congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance on the way in which he has endeavoured to help his colleague, but I think a little discipline from the other members of the government might assist the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to conduct the affairs of his department in a more businesslike way.

Mr. Chairman, I confess that I am somewhat at a loss to understand exactly the position
which the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) takes upon this question, and I am still at a loss to understand what is the position of hon. gentlemen opposite.
You had better find out where you are at yourself.

I generally have no difficulty upon that score, and if I fail the hon. gentleman is always ready to point it out. It is not worth our while to return again to the argument as to whether this is or is not a legal contract. We were all over that ground before, and it will not be profitable at this advanced stage of the session to go over it again. But suppose we admit for the purposes of argument that it is a legal and binding contract for five years, will the hon. member for Centre Toronto tell me what is wrong about it ? Where is the wrong in saying to a Canadiaii enterprise that if you will fulfil your part of the contract and make us good rails we will for five years buy from you rather than in a foreign market, always provided that you sell to us at a fair and reasonable price ? Is that not the state of the case ? I appeal to the hon. member for Centre Toronto :	Is not that the proposition before the committee, according to his own contention ?
That should be.
He says it should be. Is not that the statement of the case ?
Not as stated by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals.

The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals states and truthfully states that this is not a legal and binding contract, but we need not quibble over that. Admitting, for the sake of argument, that it is a legal and binding contract, what is that contract ? It is a declaration that for the purpose of encouraging a new industry in Canada, for the purpose of starting a business which has not hitherto existed, we will do something to help that industry, an industry in the province of the hon. gentleman which he ought to take an interest in and which he ought to be proud of. We are not going to encourage that industry by paying its promoters an extravagant price, but we simply say that if you are willing to make good rails and sell them to us at the English standard market price, we will for five years buy these rails from you rather than go abroad for them. Who should object to a thing like that ? I No mam on this side of the House wants to object, hut above all others why should hon. gentlemen opposite object who claim to be the defenders of the native industry of the country ?
What objection have I taken ? Would the hon. gentleman point out wherein I have objected ?
If my hon. friend has not been objecting for the last ten minutes, what was the purport of his speech ?
I think the purport of my speech was pretty plain.
I think so too.

The purport of my speech was that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, to begin with, had misstated the case. He had led the country to believe that there was no contract when there was a contract. He misled the House as to the terms of the contract; he misled the country a's to the understanding he had about the order in council, and after being convicted out of his own mouth he has not the manliness to come before us in a straightforward way and say that he made a mistake in stating that the contract was for 25,000 tons, when it really was for
125,000	tons. We on this side of the Hou'se are anxious that industries of every kind should be established in this country, but we blame the government for endeavouring to crush out one industry in order to establish another.

And so it appeals that the question is not whether this bargain was a good bargain or a bad bargain, but whether or not the Minister of Railways is a manly man. I have the greatest respect for my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock), but I do not think that the Minister of Railways is called on to receive any lectures on manliness from him. We are not going to waste time over questions of that kind. The only thing the people of Canada are concerned about is whether this is a good bargain for this country or not. It does not matter as to whether my hon. friend (Mr. Brock) wants to deliver a lecture to my hon. colleague (Mr. Blair), but it does matter that this government has adopted the wise and prudent policy of helping a Canadian in-'dustry by buying in the home market things which the home market can supply at a's fair a price as foreigners. My hon. friend (Mr. Brock) coming from the great province of Ontario, apparently is not anxious that this industry shall be established in that province. One would think that he should come here praising the Minister of Railways for helping to build up that native industry, instead of delivering a lecture to that hon. gentleman, in order, if possible, to induce him to abandon kite contract with Canadians and to buy his rails in a foreign market. The attitude of the hon. gentlemen opposite throughout this whole question has been an attitude of hostility to the development of Canadian industries.
Hear, hear.
[DOT]
No.

Let me tell them that there is a real encouragement of native industries and a bogu's encouragement of native industries. This government has been encouraging native industries in a legitimate way. It was a good policy to encourage the building of locomotives at Kingston as a native Canadian indutetry, but we have found nothing but nagging from hon. gentlemen opposite on that question. It is a good policy to encourage the making of steel rails in Ontario, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) and his colleagues instead of helping us have been nagging, and nagging, and nagging, in tiie hope that we would abandon that policy.
Hon. Mr. jlAGGART. The Minister of Finance is wandering from the question when he talks about the encouragement of native industries. What we say is that the Minister of Railways told us last year that there were others who were willing to furnish the government with steel rails, but perhaps they wiere not so accommodating to the hon. gentleman and the ministry immediately before the elections, and they did not get the chance of competing for the supply of these steel rails. The Minister of Railways told us last year that there were two companies who wanted to furnish steel rails, but one poor company was not consulted at all. A private bargain was made with the other company and the Minister of Finance, who I believe originated the steel works in his own province, must condemn in his heart the private bargain made with the Clergue Company which left the Nova Scotia company in the lurch. He must, in his heart, condemn the Minister of Railways, who gave to his friends five or six dollars per ton more than these steel rails could be furnished for by others. He must condemn the bargain which left out the Nova Scotia company which 'is located on the very line of the Intercolonial Railway. And, the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Brock) is blamed by these gentlemen because he disapproves of their conduct, when forsooth, as they say, they are acting on the broad, and manly, and national ground of encouraging home industries. What becomes of the native industry in Nova Scotia, and how does it happen that the government are buying rails for the Intercolonial from the further end of Ontario in order that a steel industry might be established there. The member for Toronto was told that he must [DOT] move from the narrow groove he is moving in at present and forsake the principles of his life in order that he may adopt a broad national platform and endorse this Liberal government in their policy of protection.
