The hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Brock) is told that he must take a broad survey

of tlie whole situation, and discover at Sault Ste. Marie a place where steel rails can be manufactured at a lower price than they can in the province of Nova Scotia. What nonsense that is. I had always thought that the province of Nova Scotia was particularly well situated for that industry ; that the iron mines were within a few miles of the works ; that coal was ready at hand ; and that they were not only to supply Canada with steel and iron, but that they were going to compete with our American friends for the supply of the European market. I am inclined to think that the people of Nova Scotia have some provincial instincts, and that the Minister of Finance will find it hard to get them to look at this question from the broad national view that he talks about. What I rose particularly to point out was that the Minister of Railway's told us last year that he had a communication from two steel companies.
The hon. gentleman said that I stated that the government had been negotiating with two different steel companies on the subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That is what I did say.
The MINISTER OF RxVILWAYS AND CANALS. I do not think the hon. gentleman can read that.
I will read from ' Hansard' what was said on that occasion:

The government may make any conditions they like in a contract before granting the subsidy. What an absurd clause this is, providing that the railway company will only be obliged to take the rails if they can get them as cheap as elsewhere. The railway companies will do that in any event.

It is hardly as absurd as the hon. gentleman thinks, otherwise persons contemplating establishing rolling mills for the rolling of steel rails would not attach importance to it. We have been asked by two different companies that contemplate establishing works for this purpose, to make it a condition that companies receiving subsidies from the government shall get their rails in Canada if they can get them on as favourable terms, and unless we adopt this clause it might not be possible to have manufactures of this kind started in Canada. The clause is not objectionable, and will have the effect of stimulating the manufacture of steel rails in this country.
Then, why did the hon. gentleman not give this other company a chance ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Did they make an offer ?

Who knew that the hon. gentleman wanted to purchase steel rails ? Did he advertise for tenders ? Had any one an opportunity of making an offer ? No. That was not in the'interest of the Minister of Customs and several more of hon.
gentlemen opposite in the province of Ontario at that particular time. What we object to is not the policy of having the steel; rails manufactured in the country; but what we say is that every free man and every corporation in the country has a right to compete for this service; that the contract should not be given to any one without tender or competition, and given at a very suspicious moment-a few days before an election. That is what we object to. We are proud because we are the founders of the national prosperity. What manufacturing this country has it owes to the party on this side of the House, and what is detrimental to manufactures it owes to hon. gentlemen opposite ; and if it were not that these gentlemen are obliged to follow the policy of the whole civilized world and adopt ours, swallowing their own professions, there would be a sad state of affairs in the country. What we ask for every free man in this country is the right to supply the government with the materials they require, if he can do so on as good terms as others. According to the statement of the Minister of Railways last year, there were firms in this country, two at any rate, who told him that they were prepared to manufacture steel rails. I may have been mistaken when I said that possibly one of these firms was a firm belonging to the hon. gentleman's province. He may be perfectly correct in saying that that firm never made a proposal and was not in a position to perform the work until lately. The hon. Minister of Finance said in April last that they were not in a position to do so until December. A month afterwards they were in a position to perform the work.
They are not in a position yet to perform it.
According to the statement of the Minister of Finance made in this House in April last, they were not in a position to perform it until December.

No. An hon. member referred to a document or a prospectus issued in December, in which they proposed to raise capital for the purpose of going into the steel rail business. I did not mention the word ' December' at all. It came from an hon. gentleman on the other side.

Turn up revised ' Hansard,' page 3575. The note I have says : ' Mr. Fielding reiterates the statement that it was not until December the Dominion Iron and Steel Company mentioned their intention to make rails.'
I was quoting what another hon. gentleman said, and I stated that even according to that statement it was not until December that they contemplated making rails.
It may be as the hon. minister states.
Will the hon. gentleman, while discussing this matter, inform the House what progress has been made in Sydney in the direction of manufacturing steel rails ?

I have not the slightest idea whether they intend to make steel rails or not. My argument is based on the statement of the Minister of Railways and what may he my garbled statement of the Minister of Finance.
Oh, no ; It is not garbled.

But I understood from his statement, as contained in 'Hansard,' that he admitted that they were not In a position to make an offer or to come to any decision with regard to making steel rails until December.
They have never made a proposal down to this minute.

There can be no question about the language of the hon. Minister of Railways ; and our contention on this side of the House is that it was an improvident bargain, made without competition, which is contrary to one of the doctrines of the Reform party, contrary to the law of the land, contrary to the order in council ; that all such contracts should be open to competition ; and that, even if it was made, one of the conditions of a contract involving $4,000,000 should be that before it took effect it should be approved by parliament. These are doctrines which have been again and again laid down by all the leaders of the Liberal party when in opposition and these gentlemen when in power, coolly throw over board all the professions made by the Liberal party when on this side of the House in reference to contracts, in reference to promises, in reference to economy, in reference to everything else, and have the boldness to stand up and jus-ify their conduct, and attack a friend of mine from the city of Toronto, who, in a modest and intelligent manner, states his views honestly before this House. I say that this transaction is one of the darkest. The idea of entering into a $4,000,000 contract at a fixed price of $32.60 per ton for the first 25,000 tons, and at a price for the balance according to the ruling price in England ! They know that the market is being undersold by American manufacturers. The report of the Carnegie Company, published the other day, shows that the price of rails in the United States is $6 or $7 a ton more than the price in foreign markets. In foreign markets they sell rails at a great deal less than at home. No person can justify the government in making a secret bargain with an American firm, at the particular time when this bargain was made, for the supply of steel rails for the Intercolonial for the next five years when, if the matter had Mr. HAGGART.
been open to free competition, establishments might have been created by our own people in this country capable of doing the work. Such a transaction, on the part of men who formerly expressed opinions in an entirely contrary direction when on this side of the House, cannot be justified.

The hon. gentleman commenced his attack on this item since luncheon by pointing out that this agreement was not in conformity with the order in council, and it was a very serious matter of complaint on his part that the order in council had not been more closely pursued. I gather now that the hon. gentleman feels constrained to acknowledge that that complaint is without foundation, and he has drifted on to another element of complaint, that is, that this government ought to have submitted this offer to competition, so that people disposed to start an industry for the manufacture of steel rails could enter on that work ; and he says that during the last session I stated in my place in the House that the government were negotiating then with two companies in Canada for the manufacture of steel rails for the Intercolonial Railway. I did not recollect having made any such statement. I did not believe that I could have made it, and certainly I could not have made it without knowing that that was not the fact. But the hon. gentleman was confident that on turning up ' Hansard' he could verify the correctness of his allegation, and he did turn up ' Hansard.' What followed ? It appeared by ' Hansard' that what was said on that occasion was exactly what my memory enabled me to state to the committee. When we had an explicit resolution under the consideration of parliament, I said that I did recollect that there were two people at least who had said to us that they had in contemplation the entering into the business of manufacturing steel rails.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

One of these was Mr. Clergue, representing the steel works, and the other was a gentleman who said that the Cramp people were coming into Canada and were going to establish works, and that they would take up the manufacture of steel rails. Is not the statement which the hon. gentleman has read from ' Hansard ' in absolute conformity with my recollection of it, and entirely contrary to what the hon. gentleman declared it was ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

There was not one word about the government having negotiations with any-i body for the purchase of rails. What I said , was, that we had been asked by two gentlemen representing parties who were con, templating establishing works for this pur-

pose, to make it a condition that railway companies receiving subsidies from the government should buy their rails in Canada, if they could get them on equally favourable terms as elsewhere.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is just what the hon. member for Lanark said.
Let the hon. member for Northumberland be calm. There is no occasion for intense excitement, even though he does feel a little uncomfortable under the circumstances.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is enough to make any honest man feel uncomfortable to have a minister of the Crown trying to crawl out of a statement he made to this House.
I think my hon. friend could be more dignified than he is.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And you could be more honest, but you will not.

The hon. gentleman is not doing himself justice. He is naturally a good-natured man, and is trying to create the impression that he is anything but that. Because we represented to parliament that we should incorporate a clause in our railway subsidies Act, requiring that rails, if made in Canada, should be purchased by these companies-which representation was made on a suggestion made to us-the hon. gentleman says it was our duty to have offered to the public the proposition which we ultimately agreed on with Mr. Clergue. I do not assent to anything of the kind. I do not think that such a proceeding would have been at all businesslike. My hon. friend talks about making such an agreement as this with Mr. Clergue without having invited competition. Why, the biggest contract ever made in Canada was made without any attempt to get competition, and that contract would be justified by every hon. gentleman opposite. What was our object ? Our object was to encourage an enterprise which was about to be started. The company had shown its ability to take up an enterprise of this kind and carry it out to success. Is there anybody who has done as much in the way of establishing new industries as Mr. Clergue, and who would be able to carry out the contract within the time specified ? There is nobody. Why, the gentleman who approached me in Ottawa during last session and suggested that we should put this clause in our railway subsidies Act has not been able to put on its feet yet the company which he contemplated organizing. It is not organized yet ; it is not as yet thinking of starting the manufacture of steel rails in Canada.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Which company?
The company which this gentleman who saw me expected to form, and who was one of the two gentlemen who suggested we should put this clause in our subsidy grants.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Name.

I can name the gentleman if it would be any advantage to the House to know it, but, if my memory serves me right, he was connected in some way with gentlemen who mentioned the name of Mr. Cramp. The scheme never went any further.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It was the company which was to start at Welland.

It was proposed to start at Welland, but, it has not been started yet. We could not make a contract with persons who have not yet organized, and were not prepared to undertake any contract. But, here was Mr. Clergue, whose enterprise was on its feet, successful and prosperous, and commanding unlimited capital.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would it not have been possible for the parties with whom the hon. gentleman refers, to put their company on its feet within the next four years and make steel rails ? But, he has cut them out entirely during that period.

Any company that would get the contract would require to have it for a term of years. But, we could not give any contract to a company which was not yet formed. These people, who were going to establish the industry at Welland, knew that we had inserted this clause in the railway subsidies, and if they had come, after this clause had been inserted, and said to us : Now, we have the capital and are prepared to go on and manufacture steel rails in Canada, if you will give us some encouragement, it would have been a fair proposition for us to consider whether we should not do something to help them, and whether we should not divide our contract between the two. But, we had only one company which was prepared to make us a business offer, and which we believed would be able to carry out any undertaking on which it would enter.
But that is not what my hon. friend from Lanark is seriously complaining of. He knows that the arrangement made is a good one. He knows that we will be getting good value in the rails themselves, and additional value in the fact that we will have enabled this new industry to be established. My hon. friend knows that it would not have been a business proceeding to have asked for tenders from gentlemen who had not even formed a company.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: My contention was, that the hon. gentleman should not speak one thing and think another.

I would like to inform hon. gentlemen opposite that there is no occasion for them to shed tears over the iron situation in the county of Cape Breton. When the company operating in Cape Breton was established, the promoters considered that they would have to seek foreign markets for nearly every ton of iron they produced. They did not count on sending a single ton of that iron into the Canadian market, but based all their anticipations on foreign markets. I may add that if the company in Sydney got a contract for a fraction of
25.000	tons per year, that would be a mere bagatelle in the business they propose doing. If they go into the manufacture of steel rails, they will not look to a market of
5.000	or 10,000 tons in Canada, but to South America and North and Soutn Africa and the European markets, where they hope to place scores of thousands of tons. So that the statement that the Cape Breton company was seemingly ignored really has no weight whatever.
I would also like to inform my hon. friend that if he is particularly anxious to help that industry down there, there is a project to which he can lend his powerful aid, and which will, in all probability, if carried out, conduce largely to the establishment of a large steel rail business at Sydney. I refer to the Ottawa and Georgian Bay canal, for the ore in the Lake Superior district is suitable for the manufacture of steel rails. I do not think that the hon. member for South Lanark can show that we are quite sure that the ore on which we mostly depend is by itself of the necessary quality for the manufacture of steel rails.

As to the statement of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals that the largest contract ever made in Canada was made without competition, I have always understood that it was made subject to the approval of parliament. In this important respect it is a very different contract from that which the hon. gentleman has laid on the Table. I suppose that in a moment of inadvertence the hon. gentleman forgot that. As to assisting Canadian industries, I do not think there is any question about the wisdom of that, and no one on this side has suggested that they should not be encouraged. But you can encourage Canadian industries and at the same time carry on public business as it should be carried on. The hon. gentleman said that the other company which he did undoubtedly refer to, was not the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. I had supposed that it was. but I accept his statement. But, whether it was that company or not, he knew that that company was going into the manufacture of iron on a large scale at Sydney, and he might have considered that Mr. BLAIR. .
they might extend their operations ; and, in view of that possibility, it would have been reasonable for him to take the contract for a year only and not to make one for five years, covering the entire amount required during that period by the Intercolonial Railway. This would have left him free to make such contracts as would give any encouragement thought desirable to industries in different parts of the country. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) said that this company did not require encouragement of that kind. He may be able to speak for that company, which I am not. But I should imagine that a contract for a portion of this quantity of rails would not be unacceptable to that company. I believe that the company was as far ahead with its preparations at the time the contract was made as was the company organized by Mr. Clergue.
Is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) in a position to say whether the company have iron ore suitable for the manufacture of steel rails ?

I am not an expert in iron ore. But I have it on good am thority that this company decided in September last to engage in the manufacture of steel rails, that about the first of the year they put their plans in the hands of an architect, and that they expect their works to be completed about the end of the year.
I hope we shall see it.
Has the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendall) information different from that ?
I am not in a position to give the House the information I possess.
Oh, oh.
But I will give it later on.

It is quite evident that the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) was not in this House when hon. gentlemen on the other side were in opposition, or he would have known that they objected to everything, good, bad or indifferent.
No, no.

I was here, and I speak by the book. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) says that the ore used by the Sydney plant is not suitable for the manufacture of steel rails. I think that the gentlemen who are engaged in that industry will not thank him for the advertisement he has given. Even if what he says is true it does not follow that they cannot make steel rails. But few plants have the ore in their beds from which steel rails can be made, but they supplement their own supply with importations of a more suitable quality. I am surprised that an hon. gentleman coming from the portion of the country in which these great works are situated, works of which we are all proud, should speak as he does. I can tell the hon. gentleman that while in Pittsburg I was told that the only competition that the great iron works there feared was that in Cape Breton. I hope that that is true. I hope also that at least one of these companies will not allow itself for any money to be taken over by the great steel combination, for an independent company there would be one of our great safeguards. Without desiring to dwell upon this point-though I take great pride * in it as a Canadian-I may say that the reason why this competition was feared by the Pittsburg manufacturers was that the Cape Breton works are at the seaboard and also that they have their fuel at their door-. There is nothing in what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendall) says to convince us that they cannot compete with any manufacturers in the world in the production of steel rails. For this reason, it is to be regretted that the Minister of Railways did not give this company a chance. I have it on what I consider reliable authority that as long ago as last September or October this company set aside $1,000,000 for the purpose of going into the steel industry.
They are going at it in the best way ; they are employing the best architects and are studying the best plant and methods, not making that haste which may mean less speed. Therefore, I think the minister is-fairly open to the criticism expressed by the hon. member for South Lanark, which was a fair, just and proper criticism. And it was criticism on broad and not on narrow lines. If the minister was ready to enter into a contract of this kind, he should have ascertained whether more than one steel company was ready to enter into negotiations or likely to be.
I was glad last year when I heard it mentioned, I was glad to hear he had put it into the subsidy agreements. I think he made a great mistake when he did not inquire from that company before he gave himself away-using that term in a business sense-to the Clergue syndicate. If he had done so he surely would have told us. The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) made a fair criticism when he spoke of a want of proper notice being given. But the matter was worse than that. This was done on the eve of an election. I do not think the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) needs to regret that they did not give him a chance to crow over it during the election. I am charitable enough to attribute another reason to the Minister of Railways and Canals for keeping it concealed. We of the opposition would have been glad to hear of it about election time, and to have been able to point out that the minister had made a $4,000,000 contract on the eve of an election for rails not then to be delivered. Now, I want to go back to the contract. The Minister of Finance got up and, in rather a warm tone for him, in a stentorian voice, attacked the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) for making what I think was a perfectly fair criticism. It is complained tojday because we criticise this contract. When we first heard about these steel rails there was no contract, there was no order in council mentioned, there was a verbal understanding.

I am sure the hon. gentleman does not intend to misstate the facts. He will find on referring to the statement I made when the subject was first introduced, that desiring to put the whole facts before the House, I stated that there was a contract with Mr. Clergue, or with the Lake Superior and Power Company, for one year, and there was an understanding that if we liked we would take rails from them, a similar supply, year after year for the following four years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I quite agree with that. But I think the minister gave us to understand at first that it was ,only for the one year.

I stated just what I have said now.
Hou. Mr.. TISDALE. We understood it was only Verbal. He will remember that is what he said the first time, whatever may have been drawn out of him subsequently. The same day that was first mentioned, the hon. member for Lanark asked him if there was a written contract, and then the minister said lie thought there was one.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is not correct. After I had made my statement, and while I was on my feet, the hon. member asked me if that contract would be produced, and I said yes. I certainly thought the contract was executed, and I said it would be produced. and directed the deputy minister to have it brought over.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not blaming the minister for that.
The hon. gentleman seems to desire to make out that I wilfully made a mistake.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No, I am not charging the minister with any desire to deceive. But in the first jilace we understood that he had bought 25,000 tons of rails for this year, and there had been an understanding about a further purchase. Then it transpired afterwards there was a written contract.
No, I stated that in the very first discussion that there was a contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Was there a statement made to my hon. friend from Lanark about a written contract ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Let it be so, that does not affect my argument, the point I want to make. I say it first transpired that
25,000	tons had been bought, and there was an understanding about a further purchase. Then the next statement was that the understanding was in writing.
I stated that at first.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Then the hon. member for Lanark asked to have that produced, and the minister said he would produce it. On the next occasion we had a discussion of the question whether the contract was for four years or only for one year, and different positions were taken by members of the cabinet. The Minister of Finance said there was only a moral obligation ; the Prime Minister said that the order in council settled the matter, and that it was binding ; the Minister of Railways and Canals said there was an agree-Mr. TISDALE.
ment for 25,000 tons this year, and 25,000 tons for four successive years afterwards, at prices to be fixed by the English market. The Minister of Railways and Canals said, as he says to-day, that he proposes to carry that agreement out in good faith. I am not finding any fault with him, so far as to question his always saying he would carry out the 5-year contract. I am simply giving the order of the discussion. On the second day of the discussion it transpired that the contract had been sent out, but that it bad not been executed. It had been recalled after the first discussion, and was returned unexecuted. That was the state of affairs. Now, what have we got to-day ? As the member for Centre Toronto says, today we have a new contract, a different contract, one that does not cover all the ground of the order in council, simply a contract for one year at a fixed price, with a recital from the order iu council, showing that there was some intention, at all events, of making a five years' contract. That makes all the difference in the world. What does the government mean to do ? I am surprised that they do not bring down the contract now. or the order in council confirmed by parliament, if this is to be a binding arrangement. But there seems to be a difference of opinion, even between members of the government, as to the effect of an order in council, though we have not seen any member of the government stand up and sav that he believed the country was bound 'by that order in council. Technically they may say it is not a legal obligation. The Minister of Railways and Canals has never taken that position. He says he is going to carry that out. But the Ministei of Finance, notwithstanding his warm attack upon my hon. friend, gave us to understand, by saying, no, no, when the Minister of Railways and Canals was speaking today in regard to it, that he did not consider that the government are bound to carry out this contract with the Clergue syndicate.	.
It was not made clear, though I admit that the omission was not intentional, that the rails were to be manufactured in Canada. but the inference was that they were to be. I had supposed that the government would bring down the contract* for all these years and ask parliament to ratify it. The hon. Minister of Finance rather ridiculed us for having contended that the contract was binding, although be boasted that they had made a Contract to encourage a steel rail industry in this country. Yet, what is to be the result ? How will the country understand it ? I confess that I do not understand the intention of the government. Whatever objection there may have been to their passing this order in council I think they are bound by it. and. while I object to the way in which they have done it. still I think it "should become law and be carried out in good faith. If there is any doubt

about it, and the doubts come from the colleagues of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, I had expected that we would be asked to ratify it, and that before we passed upon this item filially, we would know whether the government were to be bound by this arrangement or not. To use strong words about the criticism of my hon. friend, according to my idea, leaves confusion worse confounded. Is this a contract ? It is surely a contract for one year. The recital in it means something or it should not be put in, and yet the hon. gentleman's colleagues stand up and say that they are not bound. Do they intend to leave the matter in that shape ? I say it is not fair to them, it is not fair to the country and it is not good business. Now, suppose that the hon. gentleman went out of power.
Oh.

Hon. gentlemen may think that will not happen. I am inclined to think it will not happen this year, but suppose it did; are their successors bound to carry out this arrangement ? AVhere the government pass an order in council without the authority of the parliament, pledging the credit of the country to it; we on this side of the House, I think, very fairly have a right to object to that. I think it is a most improper thing. I think it would be improper in any government in a matter of this kind to make a contract without competition. But, granted that they are correct, that this is not a binding contract, is it good faith to the parties, or to the country, to refuse to say that we are going to make that binding whether it is binding or not ? The government seem to be divided in their own opinion about it. I dare say that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House would be divided about the binding character of the agreement in a strictly legal sense for the next four years unless parliament ratified it. When the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, at the close of the discussion, very properly and very courteously produced the contract, I confess that I was surprised when I saw that it was a. contract for one year. In view of this, it would look to me very doubtful whether there is any contract or not constituted by the order in council. The only recognition of the order in council is the recital of this agreement. I submit this point with the desire of having the matter considered; I do not submit it in a partisan spirit. I would go just as far, as any other hon. minister in the public interest to secure the recognition of a substantial industry of this kind in any province of the Dominion, and the government, having taken the responsibility of pledging the credit of the country thus far, they should, in my opinion, take the responsibility of asking this House to confirm or reject that part of the pro-1654
position that-they are still leaving in doubt, if there is any doubt about it at all. I appeal to them now to put the order in council in that shape and leave it there for the future. It is the proper course for any party or any set of ministers when they take the responsibility of a certain policy to put it in proper parliamentary form, or remove it at the earliest opportunity. I think that what I suggest is in the interest of good government, and I make the suggestion without any desire at all that there should be any further criticism than has already taken place, the question as to price having been pretty fully discussed by the two sides of the House. The only criticism that I think might be fairly made to-day in regard to the price, is that you might have stipulated for using the quotations, both in the United States and England, for the purpose of fixing the price so that you would have a larger latitude, but, still, taking the English price as it is, I would be prepared to support a proposition of that sort for the purpose of encouraging a new industry in this country. This is a great benefit, because, in addition to the price they have a protection on iron and steel rails amounting altogether to $7 a ton in addition to the price. I would not quarrel about that so much, but do not let us have this proposition go out of this House or through this House in the undecided condition in which it is. It is in the interest of the people who are going to deal with the government that we should take the course which I propose. It will not reflect credit on the country if this matter is allowed to remain in the position in which it now is, and, under these circumstances, the strongest point and the only one I care to raise is this, because the other matters have been fully discussed, that the government would do well to reconsider the matter and adopt a different course of proceeding.

The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) seems to find solace in the fact that the steel rail industry established in Cape Breton at Sydney does not need a contract of this kind, because the export trade is open to it and it would be of such immense advantage, receiving the present bounties, that it could rely entirely on that advantage.
I did not put it just in that way.

I would not care to misrepresent the hon. gentleman, because he would then have to settle it with the hon. minister, but, perhaps I had better let the hon. gentleman into a little secret, namely, that the government of the day proposed that the bounty should be confined entire-i ly to iron and steel produced for home consumption in Canada, and the hon. Minister of Finance, the spokesman of the government. when introducing his resolutions declared in unequivocal terms that boun-

ties were always considered a form of commercial hostility by foreign countries, and that, therefore, the government did not propose that these bounties should apply to any iron for export. But, after a good deal of strong criticism on this side of the House, the hon. Minister of Finance felt hound to yield, and if the manufacturers of iron and steel in Canada have any benefit, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendall) can thank this side of the House for the advantage to which he referred a moment ago. I was rather astounded at the Minister of Railways taking shelter behind the declaration that no person could make an arrangement for steel rails to be delivered during the present year at prices lower than those contained in the contract. The minister knows that is an idle challenge. He knows that he gave more than a year for the delivery of those rails under the contract. Will the minister say that he would not pay less for rails to be delivered a year hence ?
I do not think we could get them for less.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister only gives his thought on that. It may be that you cannot get them at a less price for the present year.
I am positive about that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But the minister knows that that argument is idle when applied to steel rails to be delivered a year hence. I have no hesitation in saying, and I believe the country will take the same view, that the Minister of Railways has made an improvident bargain-not improvident because it encourages Canadian industries ; but improvident because it is unfair to Canada. Canada lias given large 'bounties for the purpose of establishing this industry and the minister knows very well that parliament never intended that this bounty should be backed up by high-priced contracts in order to enable one company to swallow all the benefit. The idea of giving bounties was to encourage the steel industry generally throughout Canada, and he knows very well that this four million contract will defeat that idea.
Suppose the rails should fall in price from $36 a ton to say $20 a ton, would the hon. gentleman still say that it was a four million dollar contract ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would not.
Then why say it ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Because it is possible that the rails would advance in price and then it will be more than a four million dollar contract. Canada fulfilled its whole duty when It gave this bounty, and the intention when Mr. CLANCY.
the bounty was given was that other companies; would have an opportunity of earning it. Why did not the minister state in his contract that the governing price of the rails would be the price in Canada-because by that time we might have some other steel rail industries in Canada-or why did not the hon. gentleman include the United States ? There is no use of discussing whether this is a legal bargain or not. The minister has bound the country for one year, and he has bound the country in honour to continue that contract for a further period of years. I say here, speaking for myself, that it is our bounden duty in the interest of the people, to purchase our rails wherever we can get them at the cheapest possible price. These bounties are the most liberal that have ever been given in any country in the world for encouraging an industry of that kind, and when we gave those bounties it was the duty of the government to give others a fair chance to compete year after year so that we might buy our steel rails at the cheapest price. The constituents of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendall) will not be thankful to him for saying that they have not iron in Nova Scotia suitable for making steel rails. If he goes to the town of Sydney and makes a statement of that kind I rather think his reception will not be very enthusiastic.

I am in the habit of making the same statement in one place as in another, and every statement I have made here to-day I have made in Sydney, a little stronger. I will explain that to the hon. gentleman later on.

Then I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendall) has more courage than judgment. With the great advantages they have at Sydney, there will probably be a steel rail industry established there within a year. They will have to depend on their export trade to make a profit, just as the Lake Superior Power Company wiU have to depend on the export trade after this contract has expired. However that may be, every industry in Canada should have an equal opportunity of competing for the supply of the Canadian market. The people of the country will regard this as an extremely improvident 'bargain, and the sentiments given utterance to by my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Brock) are entirely in consonance with the public opinion of the country. I challenge the Minister of Railways to say that he cannot make a bargain to-day to have steel rails delivered fourteen months hence and at an infinitely better price than the price mentioned in this contract.

Of course I cannot say that without making inquiries, but I think it would not be possible to make a contract to-day for delivery next week at any less price than the contract we made last August. I believe "that, although I will not assert it with

the same confidence as I make the other statement which is the result of information given me by reliable parties. I believe that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) is taking an attitude in which his friends on that side of the House will not assume the responsibility of supporting him. He says that such a proposition as this which has been made to Mr. Clergue's company, made with the object of, encouraging the establishment of a new industry, ought to be made subject to conditions which would throw that company open to competition with the rail manufacturers of the United States. I ask my hon. friend to put his view on that question in the form of a motion before this House, and find how many supporters ho will get on his own side.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow me ? I am prepared to speak for myself, and I do not think I run counter to the opinions of hon. members on either side of the House, nor -speak at variance - with good sense, when I say that the people of Canada are entitled to buy from Great Britain, from Canada, or from the United States, at the best price possible, and save the public purse.

lt OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. The hon. gentleman has not qualified in the slightest degree the language which I attributed to him. I repeat the suggestion I made a moment ago. True, the hon. gentleman says these are his own words ; but has he enough confidence that his view on this question will find any sort of 'support to put a motion before the House embodying that view, and challenge an expression of opinion upon it ? I make this prediction, that if the hon. gentleman deos so, he will not have a corporal's guard to support him, and why ? Because any one who has any knowledge of the actions of the manufacturers of the United States knows that they will cut prices on goods which are to be exported to Canada below the price's at which they are selling to home consumers. I know that from my little experience with them in the purchase of steel rails on behalf of the government. I made a bargain with ia manufacturer in the United States for rails at $32.00 a ton when there was not a purchaser of rails in the United States who could get them for less than $35. They were willing to cut $2.40 to our advantage, because the rails were coming into Canada. And does my hon. friend suppose that any persons whose bona fide object was to establish an industry for manufacturing rails in Canada could fairly be asked at the outset to meet in competition the cut prices of the manufacturers of the United States ? If such a '[DOT]suggestion were made to them, what would be the answer ? It would be: Gentlemen, we will not undertake the business. And so, when we had our negotiations with the Lake Superior Power Company, they said: ' We cannot go into this business if you make it. a condition that we shall be subject to competition with the LTnited States. Make it the open market in England, and we will do it.' Could anything be fairer or juster than that ? I again ask my hon. friend, if lie is willing to take the responsibility of standing up to the view he has expressed ns to what the government should have done in this contract to table a resolution embodying that view, and invite the support of parliament for it.
Oh, rubbish.

It Is no more rubbish than the opinion expressed, and I am not going to say that that is rubbish ; but I want the hon. gentleman, if he is prepared to take the responsibility of attacking the action of the government, to find out just what parliament thinks of his view. My hon. friend has another ground of complaint. He said it was improper for the government to give a contract in this form and for this purpose to a company which, in manufacturing its iron and steel, would already be in receipt of a large bounty from the government. I understood my hon. friend to speak of the bounty as an outrageous or excessive bounty.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Surely the hon. gentleman will not make that statement. I said the bounty was a very proper one, that I was in favour of it: but I said that it gave the iron industry of Canada immense advantages, all the advantages that we were bound to give in purchasing our steel rails, and that any further advantages would be at the expense of the public purse.

I shall be very ready to acknowledge the fact if I have misquoted or misrepresented the language of the hon. gentleman. I thought he said that we were giving this company an extremely liberal contract. What was in the hon. gentleman's mind when he emphasized that ? That they got all they had a right to expect under any circumstances. Whether he meant it or not, the hon. gentleman's language would convey the impression to any one who heard him that the granting of the bounty did not meet with his very hearty approval. But my hon. friend does not want to convey that idea. My hon. friend is in favour of giving to steel and iron companies the most liberal treatment by bounty. Well, what does he propose to do ? When we have established an industry for the manufacture of iron and steel in a crude shape, would he be disposed to sit down and say: ' There is no policy which I am prepared to adopt even to the

extent of giving to these people a preference over foreign manufacturers at the same price ; there is no aid which I am prepared to offer to any of these companies to induce them to go into any allied or connected industries, no matter how valuable they tmay be, for the reason that they have already received a bounty on their iron and steel.' But if they venture to come to us and say :
' We are turning out the steel in the raw form, and we would like to manufacture it into structural iron and rails ; we would like to put the labour of Canada upon this ; we would like to put up large industries which would employ large numbers of people and circulate large amounts of money ; but we cannot do it, because unfortunately we shall have to compete again'st the products of the United States without any duty, unless you as a government, in your purchases of materials, are willing to give us some advantage over outside producers. What should we say, in the opinion of the hon. gentleman? 1 No, we will not have your allied industry ; we will not have your steel rails ; we will not have these additional men employed in Canada: because you have already received a bounty on your iron and steel in the crude form ; but with regard to anything else, do not come*to us with the suggestion that we should give you more than equal terms with outside manufacturers.' I ask my hon. friend to put that view of his in writing, and challenge the judgment of parliament upou it ; then we will see how far my hon. friend is justified in criticising the action of the government, and how far his view is sustained by those who usually act with him.
My hon. friend has suggested that we have handed over the whole steel rail business to the Clergue Company. He would lead us to suppose that the supply of 25,000 tons of rails a year for five years is a quantity so vast that it is going to overwhelm everybody, and cut a large figure in the rail supply of the world. He is allowing his feelings to run away with his judgment, and exaggerating altogether the magnitude of this proposal. What kind of a rail mill do you suppose you would be able to establish, if the extent of its business were to be limited to 25,000 tons a year ? Why, that quantity would not be a feather weight in the business of an ordinary manufacturing establishment, and a project simply for the purpose of establishing a company to manufacture steel rails to that extent would not be worth discussing for a moment. When that company is fairly established, it will turn out nearer 200.000 tons of steel rails per year than 20,000 tons. For this quantity, it has to find a market, and the government are not the only purchasers of rails in Canada. The Grand Trunk Kailway Company wants 50.000 tons at once, and the Canadian Pacific Railway is buying all the time. Numerous railways are, I am happy
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
to say, being built all over Canada, and all these must be supplied with steel rails, and outside of Canada there are reasonable expectations that markets will be found which will absorb a large quantity, and I have no doubt that these expectations will, to some extent at all events, be realized. But, the certainty of an outlet for 25,000 tons per year for five years is sufficient to give a sufficient impetus to start the company, which would not otherwise have been started, and it is being started without cost to the people of Canada. And besides, we are getting the rails we require on as favourable terms as we could get them in London, where all competitors meet.
My hon. friend from South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) does not agree with many hon. gentlemen on his own side. He is entirely in favour of this proposition. He is not criticising it on the ground taken by some of his friends who have spoken. He wants us to make the contract stronger. He has no fault to find with our encouraging this industry. On the contrary, that is entirely in accord with his judgment. He shakes himself clear of his colleagues in that particular, but, what he wants is to have this contract made stiff and hard for five years. He wants it nominated in the bond, that it shall be for five years, at the rate of 25,000 tons each year. I can well understand why the hon. gentleman should take that view, but there are reasons against it which we deem more cogent. I would have liked to have had the contract as my hon. friend suggests, but we had to weigh the question in all its bearings, and we did not feel justified in making any proposal to the Lake Superior Power Company extending over so long a period. We-felt that we would be justified in making the contract for one year, and in giving the assurance that this government, if it should live to carry it out, would see the company through to the extent of an order for five years for 25.000 tons more per year. And when that proposition was made to Mr. Clergue he accepted it. He did not ask for any more, and he is getting all that we stipulated to give him. When I tell my hon. friend that Mr. Clergue is well content with this, that he has no fault to find with either the terms of the order in council or the contract as it is now drawn, and has declared the intention of his company to execute it. I would ask my hon. friend whether, under the circumstances, he would not feel like withdrawing any opposition he might have to the contract on the ground that it does not go further than Mr. Clergue asked us to go ? My hon. friend will not be stronger in his desire, I am sure, that Mr. Clergue's interests should be protected than is Mr. Clergue himself.
There is a difficulty which would always arise if we were to make the contract for a term of five years, and that is, as to the fixing of the price from year to year. Mr. MAY 15, 1901
Clergue might very well complain that what we held was the market price of England, unless we had the price specified in writing from year to year, was not a fair statement of the market price. So that, I consider that, under all the circumstances, there can be no reasonable exception taken to the clauses as drawn ; and inasmuch as the person most interested is perfectly content,
I do not see why my hon. friends opposite should feel any more concern on the subject.
I am sure that the House, which has a pretty good memory, will be astounded at the statement of the hon. gentleman. Why, he declared that the life of that industry depended upon this contract.
I said the starting of it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: He declared that two things were absolutely necessary. One was that they should have a contract for the five years, and the other was, that the company should have no foreign competition. Yet, he tells us that it is a mere bagatelle, what they are going to supply Canada with.
Supply the government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How is he going to reconcile that statement with the other one, that the life of the industry, the fact whether it should start or not, depends upon its having a contract covering five years ? Then, he declared this afternoon that the company should be free from the competition of the United States. The hon. gentleman has a most extraordinary faculty of blowing hot and cold that I ever knew anybody to possess. Let me tell the hon. gentleman further, that he has forgotten wliat was stated in this House by the Minister of Finance, namely, that the large bounties-to which I have no objection-given are intended as compensation for having lowered the protective duties on iron. Does tne hon. gentleman mean to blow hot and cold in this case as well as the other ? Does he challenge the statement of the Minister of Finance, who declared that the increase in the bounty was to compensate for the lowering of the customs duties ? He said that we must give these people some compensation for the protection they are loosing by the reduction in duties.
Not on rails. The hon. gentleman knows that there is no duty on rails, and, therefore, we could not withdraw the protection from it.

The hon. Minister of Railways said a moment ago, that because there was no duty on steel rails, foreign rails could come into competition with Canadian rails and kill the whole home industry. Let me ask him to refer to the hon. gentleman who sits beside him-a gentleman of
high standing and great ability in this country-who, for years, has declared that there should not be any duty to protect any industry, but that the workingmen should be left to take care of themselves. Let them, he said, eat less and work longer. Now we have his colleague rising and telling us how important it is that our workingmen should have employment.
For eighteen years these hon. gentlemen fought for the views which formerly they expressed, but they were overcome, they were subdued. And now they are like a certain kind of birds, of the hawk tribe, I believe, who do not build nests of their own, but, when other birds built nests, come and take possession of them. The hon. gentleman cannot accuse us of being untrue to the principle of protection, of not showing our anxiety that employment should he provided for the workingmen. We have fought that battle and won it. But, so far as I am concerned-and I am willing to take the responsibility of my utterance-I think that we have amply done our duty by the bounties that have been given for the manufacture of iron and steel, and that by these bounties we have offered every encourage-meut for the establishment of industries that would give employment to labour. And what is our next duty ? Our next duty is to protect the taxpayers of this country. I am but an humble member of this House, and I do not assume to believe that my views are generally shared, but I have as much faith in them as though I had a majority with me. I say we have done our duty in the encouragement of this industry, and row the hon. gentleman who is in the position of the custodian of the public purse should see to it that the rights of those who contribute to the public revenues are protected. If any arrangement such as this that we are discussing had been made tdn years ago when hon. gentlemen opposite were not in power, what would they have said ? They would have pointed out that our manufacturers were given an advantage of six or seven dollars a ton, and why should they not compete against the American manufacturers ? I can Imagine with what eloquence they would have appealed to popular sentiment on that ground. I am sure the hon. minister has not improved his position by the statement that he has made, and that the public will not share his views.

I desire to speak only a word in explanation. Either I was unfortunate in my expressions or the hon. minister did not understand what I said. My point was that if the government has made an order in council that was intended to be binding, they should ask the House to confirm it, making it into an agreement, or reject it. But I started by saying that fault had been found with the criticism passed upon the minister. I declared that some of the criticisms of the hon. member

for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) were to be endorsed, and I said that if the hon. minister had made the price in future years the price in a competitive market and not the market of London alone, it would have improved the order. But I said, and I say again, that I am reartily in accord with making an arrangement on some such lines as this. But if the government is pledging the good faith of the country, let us understand it, let us understand whether this is a contract which ends in a year, or whether it extends beyond that time.

I suppose it is hardly necessary to point out toj hon. gentlemen opposite that the criticisms are not all on the same line. If I understand the hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale), he his satisfied with the contract, but thinks it should be made stronger. But the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) takes the ground that, having given a bounty on the manufacture of iron and steel, our duty ceases, and that it is improper for us to enter into a contract with Mr. Clergue's company or any other Canadian company without submitting them to the competition of the United States as well as of Great Britain. I think, as the hon. Minister of Railways said, the hon. member for Bothwell is probably very much alone in that opinion. But I would point out to the hon. member for South Norfolk and the hon. member for South Lanark, that for many years it has been a question in this country whether it was advisable to put a duty on steel rails or not. Hon. gentlemen opposite claimed that they brought many industries into existence in this country by means of a protective tariff. But when it was suggested in years gone by that a duty should be placed on steel rails, as they will remember, the argument on their own side a s' well as on ours, was that steel rails were not produced in the country, but the country needed railroads, and that it was important that these railroads should be constructed at a price that would enable them to carry freight and passengers at moderate rates. It was argued that a duty on rails would enhance the cost of constructing railways, and that it would be impolitic to encourage the manufacture of steel rails in this country by the imposition of heavy duty. Had hon. gentlemen opposite followed, in the case of this industry, the same course as they did in others, they would have placed a duty of 30 per cent, say, on steel rails, thus increasing the price of steel rails, according to the import price, by from $8 to $10 per ton. This would have been) a constant burden upon the railway interest, upon the thousands and thousands of miles of railway in this country needing renewal.
Did the present government make steel rails free ?

Steel, rails were free. But this government have Mr. TISDALE.
taken action which they thought would be sanctioned by the House, and which they still believe will be so sanctioned, by which, without increasing the cost of the article to the consumer, they will be able, as they believe, to bring this industry into existence. This object will be satisfactory to men of all shades of politics. As I say, it has been done without cost to the country, without burdening the thousands of miles of track of the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk and other railroads also, and without burdening the treasury of the country, except so far as they have bound themselves not to go to the United States at particular times and buy steel rails for Canada at slaughter prices. But do hon. gentlemen say that it was right and proper that we should not enter into a contract to secure the desirable object that we have secured without stipulating that these people must submit themselves to competition at slaughter prices ? The member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) alone, so far as I have seen, has taken that view. Well, then, if it is not to be a slaughter price, if it is to be a fair price, if it is to be this year $32, and if next year the price in England is $25, and if during the whole term the price conies down to $20, then does the hon. gentleman say we are to be blamed because we have brought this important industry into existence in the way we have done ?
He alludes to what the Minister of Railways and Canals has said, and thinks he sees a contradiction in it. The minister says that this agreement made between the government and Mr. Clergue was the means of starting this enterprise, and he professes to find a distinction between that and the statement made later by the minister that this quantity was a mere bagatelle as compared with the consumption of rails in the whole world as well as in Canada. There is nothing inconsistent in the two statements. The hon. gentleman knows that 25,000 tons of steel rails are a very insignificant amount compared with the total quantity used on the railway mileage in Canada. I suppose they would rail about 200 miles of railway. But the Minister of Finance says we have 17,000 miles of railway in existence in Canada !ilone. Parliament in its wisdom has voted bonuses for hundreds upon hundreds of miles, much of which is in course of construction, and it is stipulated in these contracts-and this was a departure last year from the principles laid down by gentlemen opposite-that the companies receiving these bonuses should buy their rails of Canadian make, provided they could buy them on as fair terms in Canada as elsewhere. Now the Clergue company has been brought into existence by this government agreeing to take 25,000 tons of steel rails from them this year at a price that hon. gentlemen opposite have to admit was fair, the English price, which the Minister of Railways and Canals says is the American price to-day, if we add

the freight. We are to take 25,000 tons next year, and 25,000 the year after, the prices to be determined by the price in the open London market. That contract has brought this enterprise into existence. It needed that encouragement, that little stimulus. And I think, whatever the hon. gentleman's view may be, that the people of Canada will sanction the arrangement as an excellent one. As far as the government is concerned, they are only glad this discussion has taken place in the House, and they will be happy to have it renewed in the country. They will be happy to have the member for Bothwell go on the public platform and say that he did not think this industry should be established unless the government had obliged Mr. Clergue to submit to slaughter prices in the United States. I think I hear some of his own people saying to him : Have not you and your party been continually attacking the government because they were letting goods come into Canada from the United States at slaughter prices ? Did you not demand that the Tory party should raise the duty 15 or 20 per cent higher for that very purpose ? And yet you hold to-day that Mr. Clergue should be subjected to that competition. I fancy the people will say : When you have fixed the competitive price, when you have put Mr. Clergue in competition with the whole world for the price of steel rails, yau have done all that the interests of the country require. Mark you, Mr. Chairman, the government, in fixing the London price, does put Mr. Clergue in competition with the whole world, whatever the price may be year after year, just as the Minister of Railways and Canals and railway companies make English contracts year after year, stipulating the rails shall be at the fair market price each year. Will he say that this bargain should not have been made, that because we have given a bounty upon iron and steel, therefore we should not have secured what we have secured ? But this parliament has done more. The railways that are being built will be customers in the market. Hon. gentlemen have talked about the Sydney company. They have changed their basis to-day, the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals says that we have shut out other Canadian firms. Why, no other Canadian firm has made any proposition, nobody has been injured. Is the Sydney company complaining to-day ? Has anybody complained to the hon. gentlemen ? Nobody whose money is invested in steel rail enterprises has complained.
Yes.
Who are they ?
The government knows better than we do.
The Sydney company, for one.
Where is the evidence ?
In the pocket of the Minister of Finance.

I do not know whether the hon. gentleman is as well acquainted with my pocket as he thinks he is, but if he knows of any evidence that the Sydney company has objected, I would like to have it. If this Sydney company is complaining I would be glad to have the evidence.
Does the hon. gentleman deny that after the contract was published the Sydney company wished to share in the contract ?
I cannot deny it, because I never heard a word of it to this minute.

I can deny it, I can produce the evidence that the Sydney company communicated on the subject, and said that we ought to make sure that the rails were made in Canada. But they had no fault to find at all with the contract, and did not want it. All they wanted was that we should make sure to give the Canadian manufacturers a fair chance, to make sure that the rails were not imported from the United States.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the minister deny that a proposition was made to Mr. Clergue's company to share his contract with the Sydney company ?

I do not deny it, because I do not know it, I never heard of it before, directly or indirectly. I venture to say, however, that the Sydney company never made any such proposition, and are not in a position to make any such proposition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
We are not in a position, at least I am not, to know what information hon. gentlemen opposite may have. If they have information that was not before the government when they made this agreement, of course they cannot blame the government for having been ignorant of it. But you have heard What the Minister of Railways and Canals has said in that regard. But suppose we admit the Sydney company are about to manufacture steel rails, we are told that they have made uo preparation in that direction yet But we hope they will make steel rails, we would be glad if other companies can be promoted who will do that. Will these hon. gentlemen say to us that when, nearly a year ago, a proposition was made by which we saw that we could establish this industry in this country, we should not have taken any action then ? Does he say that we should not have taken any steps, that we should have waited until this year before taking any step, when there has not been an effort

made even yet towards the erection of a mill anywhere else Does he say that we should have waited, waited and waited until three or four mills should be established '! Why we could not have accomplished our object in that way We saw an opportunity, without costing anything to the people of Canada, without injury to any Canadian industry, so far as we can see, of bringing into existence a steel rail industry But admitting that the Sydney company are entering upon the manufacture of steel rails, that other companies are entering upon the manufacture of steel rails, as the Minister of Railways and Canals has said, would they refrain from entering upon it just because they have not secured a contract for 25,000 tons of rails when the whole world will be their market as well as Canada ? It seems to me it is idle to talk in that way. We know that hon. gentlemen opposite did talk about the great things they were going to accomplish in that direction, but they never accomplished anything. They talked about the development of the iron industry, and it all amounted to comparatively nothing, but when this government changed the terms of the bounty the whole industry sprang into existence, and it is now being carried on under this government.

The hon. Minister of Customs says that we have got this industry without cost to the country. Let me ask him. who pays the $150,000 bonus that you give to the manufacturer by way of bounty on the steel rails ?
Not a copper.
There is a bounty on pig iron of $5 a ton.
Six dollars a ton.
Six dollars a ton on 25,000 tons would make $150,000 a year.

There is a bounty on pig iron and steel billets, but does an hon. gentleman of the business experience and capacity of the hon. member from Centre Toronto say that it would be iniquitous for us to make this bargain with any othe? company or two companies ?
I am merely finding fault with the hon. gentleman's statement, that you have established this industry in the country without any cost to the country.
Yes, that is what I say.
I take issue with you there.
They get a bounty on pig iron and steel billets.
Who pays it ?
They can ship the billets away without making steel rails at all.
Yes, they can ship the steel billets if they like.
The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals told us another story.
There is no doubt that there is a bounty paid for the manufacture of steel billets.
By whom ?
By the people of Canada.
That is my only contention.
The hon. gentleman is making the contention that it is an additional charge on the people because we have bought 25,000 tons of steel rails.
You are speaking of having started a new industry in this country without any cost to the country.
Yes.
Steel rails, I suppose, cannot be made without pig iron ; therefore, you give $6 a ton to establish that industry.
I need not point out to the hon. gentleman that we can pay a bounty on pig iron and steel billets without paying it on steel rails.
You cannot pay it without taking it out of the pockets of the people of this country.
Well, it is not worth while arguing that point. We have to pay bounties on pig iron and steel billets ; we know that.
You could not say that we do not.
The hon. gentleman's argument, if it means anything, means that instead of Canada making these steel rails there should not be one pound of steel rails made in this country.
No, Sir.

That is his argument. Well, now we differ with him. We say that we have done well in having brought this industry into existence. But. I would say right here, that the steel rail industry at Sydney, or any other industry that may be started, will not be debarred by the fact that the contract for
25,000	tons' of rails has been given to Mr. Clergue. They have the market of Canada, and they will go into it if they see that it is a business enterprise. They are not debarred in any way at all. The government believe if they had not made this agreement with Mr. Clergue, we would not have had the steel rail industry advanced to the stage it has reached at Sault Ste. Marie. We might have gone on for years without

securing the establishment of this great industry. We have not done this in a way to impose a burden on the railways of the country. We are leaving rails on the free list. We are buying steel rails at the usual market price in London, England, as cheaply as anybody can get them, and we have secured a new industry. The government are not on their defence. The government are aggressive. We claim credit for having done what we have done, and we know
that the country will sustain us. We are >
in this country, giving employment to a
paying a bounty on iron. We have secured the establishment of these industries and the money paid for their construction. We have done more. While $4 a ton duty was paid on pig iron, we have reduced it to 52.50 a ton. While there was at one time $13 a ton on steel products, afterwards reduced to $10 a ton, we further reduced the duty in the interest of the consumers of this country, and the workers in iron and steel to $7 a ton. So that, while paying a bounty on iron and steel, we have relieved the consumers and the workers of this country on the other hand by reducing the tariff. And as these industries go on and develop, we will be able to reduce the burdens on the people to a greater degree than they are at the present time. This is on the record, and there is no use of arguing it any further. Hon. gentlemen opposite have admitted that the price of the rails, with the freight added, will be precisely the same as if they had been bought in the English market.

Who admitted that ?
will be a lower price. This government believe that, having brought this industry into existence, that the iron industry having been developed to the extent it has been, and whether it would be so or not was doubtful, that this industry having been established with the promise of other industries coming into existence, as hon. gentlemen opposite have admitted, by virtue of the iron industry prospering as it is doing to-day, having brought new life into an immense locomotive works
large number of people, and accomplishing this while getting goods at a fair price, as far as steel rails are concerned, in the open markets of the world-I say, that the government, having done this, feel that they have done something which will meet with the approval of the country. I am glad that this discussion has taken place, and that this' criticism has been offered, because the people of the country will see how very far the critics vary from one another in their criticism, and how their criticism has been finally disposed of by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. They will also see the great benefit that has been secured for Canada, virtually without cost to the people of this country.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 106) respecting the South Shore Railway Company.-Mr. Geoffrion.

I wish to draw the attention of the House to two clauses of this Bill, sections (c) and (d), particularly. To enable me to discuss the matter I have to go back to 1893 to find the origin of the South Shore Railway Company. In that year the Taillon government of Quebec granted a subsidy of $100,000 to the Tour-ville syndicate, which "was composed of the Hon. Mr. Tourville, Mr. Beauchemin and others. In 1894 that syndicate applied to the Quebec legislature for a charter to build a railway to be called the South Shore Railway, from a point near St. Lambert to L<ivis. As there was then a charter for a railway in the same direction, called the Great Eastern Railway, and work was done at Yamaska and Nicolet, I opposed that Bill. We came together; Mr. Tourville and Mr. Beauchemin representing the syndicate, Mr. Beemer and I representing the creditors of the Great Eastern Company, the members for Nicolet, the Hon. Mr.- Beaubien, then Minister of Agriculture, and the Hon. Mr. Nantel, Minister of Railways and Public Works. It was understood then that we should allow the syndicate to obtain the charter, and in consideration they were to purchase the South Eastern, at a cost of $70,000. The syndicate did not see its way to pay over $60,000, and therefore the government took $10,000 out of the $100,000 voted to pay the debts. Another condition was that Mr. Beemer and myself should become directors of that road. We see in the preamble of the Act ineori pointing the South Shore Railway Company the names of the Hon. Louis Tourville, Joel Leduc, .1. M. Fortier and J. R. Wilson, of Montreal, H. J. Beemer, contractor, of Montreal. H. Beauchemin, of Sorel, and George Ball, of Nicolet. At that time the Montreal and Sorel Railway, now the South Shore Railway, belonged to Messrs. Tourville and Leduc, but they had not the title of sale. They contrived to seize the road and have it sold so as to obtain a title to it. So, when the bargain to which I have referred took place, we decided to have the Montreal and Sorel sold by auction, as well as the Great Eastern Railway. Mr. Armstrong was to purchase the Great Eastern for the costs of the court, and Mr. Tourville was to get the Montreal and Sorel for the costs of the court. The time came for the Montreal and Sorel road to be sold. I was present, and Mr. Tourville bought it for $1,500, exactly the costs of the court. A few days afterwards, the time came for the sale of the Great Eastern; but instead of it being sold, as the Montreal and Sorel was. Mr. Beauchemin engaged a bidder, and the price went up to $20,000. Mr. Armstrong got the Mr. SPEAKER.
road for that price. But he could not pay the $20,000; so everything has remained in statu quo ever since, and neither the Great Eastern nor the South Shore have succeeded in having a subsidy from the government. I remember that once a large delegation came here to see the Prime Minister, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He was not Sir Wilfrid then, but he was as great as he is to-day. We had a special train, something like what we had the other day to go down to Quebec. dVe came before the government, and the speakers, instead of arguing the advantage that there would be in having a railroad passing alongside of the St. Lawrence and crossing over the bridge at Longueuil, only argued against Mr. Armstrong. Mr. Armstrong was this, and Mr. Armstrong was that, the Great Eastern could not be built, and this, and that, and no more. I recollect very well the answer of the Prime Minister. This is in substance what he said :	' Well, gentlemen, there are three
charters for railways from Quebec to Montreal: there is the Drummond County, the South Shore, and the Great Eastern. The late government have put us in a bad fix by granting two charters to go in the same direction, and now we do not know what to do. I tell you that the best thing to do is to depend on the wisdom of the government.' Coming out I met Mr. Beauchemin, and said to him: 'Well, Mr. Beauchemin, what do you think about the delegation ? ' ' Oh,' he said, ' it went very well it looked favourable; you and Mr. Armstrong will get each a nutshell and the Drummond County will get the kernel.' In 1899, Mr. Raymond Prefontaine was one of the directors of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway Company. As he had a great deal of influence with the government, we asked him on the part of the creditors of the Great Eastern Railway to get subsidies for the South Shore and also for the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway, and to sell to Mr. Beauchemin that part of the road that we could not succeed in selling in 1894. He was authorized to sell it for $70,000. the price that was stipulated before. This $70,000 was to be divided as follows :	Mr. Prdfontaine, in consideration of the great influence he had, was to receive $42,000. and pay liabilities which he had towards the bank by endoring notes for the Atlantic and Lake Superior.	The balance was to
go to other parties.	Mr. Beemer was to
have got $7,000. Mr. George Ball was to have got $3,500 out of the debt of $20,000 which he had against that road. Mr. Archibald Campbell was to have received $1,500, and the balance was to have gone to the labouring men and the engineers.
