I said a while ago that this road was to have been sold by auction so as to give a good title to the South Shore Railway Company. Mr. Prefontaine had a judgment against it, and he it was who had it sold in 1894. And as Mr. Armstrong, who bought

it in, never paid the price, Mr. Prefontaine had it said again by folle enchere. He paid $510 for it, and no one made any opposition.
Now let us see what the creditors have received from Mr. Prefontaine. For my part, I received nothing. Mr. Beemer says he received nothing. Mr. Campbell says the same thing. But there is something more serious. Mr. Prefontaine did not even pay the notes which have his name on their backs and which he was to pay out of the proceeds. Here is one of these notes.
Bead it.

It reads thus :
$4,000.	Montreal, Feb. 3, 1899.
One month after date, we promise to pay to the order of C. N. Armstrong four thousand dollars at the office here.
President.

Secretary.
On the back of the note are a number of names, nearly all dead-heads. They are : C. N. Armstrong, A. C. Wurtele, attorney ; G. R. Thibaudeau, R. Prefontaine, George Ball, James Baxter.
I paid that note, and asked Mr. Prefontaine to pay at least his share as endorser, and he refused. It has been in the hands of my lawyers since the spring, and the matter has remained in abeyance ever since in the hope that Mr. Prefontaine would come to terms.
There are other notes to the same effect. They are for $42,000 and are similar to the one I have read, only with different names on them, but they also carry Mr. Prefon-taine's name. Mr. Prefontaine wanted by that sale to get clear of all these notes. He got the money, and he got others to pay the notes.
The hon. gentleman was a director of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Company, but as soon as this transaction was put through, he resigned his position as director. He could not live any longer where Mr. Armstrong was. And it is since that date that Mr. Armstrong is, in his opinion, such a rogue.
Hon. gentlemen have noticed that Mr. Prefontaine attended the meetings of the committee when the Atlantic and Lake Superior Act was before that committee for amendment, in the interests of the trustees. You know how Mr. Prefontaine opposed the Bill. Why ? Because he wanted the Baie des Chaleurs road to be sold. Of course he knew that in that event there was an opportunity for great profit. But in spite of all his opposition, the Bill, amended if you like, passed the committee.
As soon as he resigned his directorship, he got some others to make an application for a charter for a road from Paspebiac to GaspS Basin, and he obtained a subsidy for
the South Shore Railway from Sorel down to Lotbini&re at the rate of $3,200 per mile, He succeeded in getting $35,000 for the bridge at Sorel ; $50,000 for the bridge at Yamaska; $50,000 for the bridge at St. Francois, and $15,000 for the Nicolet bridge. The piers on the Nicolet bridge were built, which cost about $35,000. and that is why its subsidy was smaller than those given the other bridges.
He also obtained a subsidy for the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway. He was to have obtained it from Paspebiac to Gaspe Basin, but after resigning the position of director, he changed his mind and he obtained the subsidy from Oaplan to Paspebiac. He obtained from Paspebiac to Gaspfi Basin a subsidy for a road the name of which was not given. Here is Bill No. 70 of last session to incorporate the Gaspe Short Line Railway Company. This is a charter which he wanted to get, but he did not succeed. There is a clause in it authorizing him to buy the Baie des Chaleurs and the Atlantic and Lake Superior. Now, Mr. Chairman, I have said all I wanted to say. I do not wish to obstruct the passage of this Bill. The House may conform to the deeds on the part of Mr. Beauchemin if they like. He has done his duty in paying what he agreed, and I think it would not be fair to deprive him of his rights. I leave the matter in the hands of the House, after explaining the matter. I wish I had a better command of English, and I would have explained it in a way that would have caused the House to understand it better. But I have done the best I could, and I leave the matter in the hands of the House.

I do not think I should take up the time of this House in discussing this Bill. We have only an hour for private Bills and my hon. triend from Nicolet (Mr. Ball) has made a long speech. The Bill was fully discussed in the Railway Committee, and that committee is so numerous that everybody is familiar with the question. From what I could gather of the speech of my hon. friend from Nicolet, he is objecting ,to the ratification of one of the deed's. In the Bill, we ask the ratification of three deeds of purchase by the present company of portions of roads for which they have paid, and for which they hold authentic deeds. The only deed to which the hon. gentleman objected, as far as I understand, was the purchase of the Great Eastern. Well, as he said, Mr. Armstrong had that part of the raod 'sold by the sheriff and bought it in ; but he could not pay the price, and the road was resold and Mr. Prefontaine bought it. It was a perfect and open sale. Mr. Armstrong was there as were all the interested parties, and they had a. right to bid. The contract was given by the sheriff to Mr. Prefontaine. The most perfect deeds that can be got are those given by the sheriff, as everybody

knows. We are in possession of those deeds. They were filed in committee, they have been discussed, everybody knows what they are. My hon. friend (Mr. Ball) says that there seems to have been a different agreement made by Mr. Prefontaine when he bought that part of the road. Mr. Prefontaine denie's that. But even if it were so that has nothing to do with the contract he has from the sheriff. They say there was a verbal agreement. If they have any rights, let them enforce them in the courts and not come to this House, which cannot learn the facts. There is nothing to prevent this House ratifying the deeds which are held from the sheriff, and that is all we ask with regard to that matter. We ask also for a few years more to complete the road. We have shown in committee that we had a right to that, and the committee recognized the fact.

In the Railway Committee this Bill attracted our attention owing to the variety of purchases and sales and bargains, and the number of jobs that seem to be connected with it. It is one of the Bills that have a history that would be interesting if one had time to study it, and get the information to enable him to understand it. But the gravamen of the case seems to be that we are asked by this Bill to ratify certain sales. Here are four sales we are asked to ratify, not one bargain of which was before us nor any information concerning it. In the committee we could get no information that would enable one to pass upon the measure intelligently. Yet, we are asked to ratify these sales, to declare that they are proper, to make them binding no matter who is cut out of his honest rights or what rascally transaction they may represent. This is one of the kind of Bills 'that, in my judgment, parliament should never pass. An effort was made to prevent it passing in the committee, but the Bill was voted through ; and now it is sent to this House and we are asked to approve it. I am sure that if one-third of the members had any intelligent knowledge of the transactions connected with this Bill, and what they are asked to make valid, the Bill would be thrown out of the House as soon as we could vote upon it.

I also desire to enter my protest against passing legislation of this kind in this House. I am sure it would take a Superior Court judge and half a dozen lawyers three weeks or a month to unravel the difficulties in connection with the title of this property. But, notwithstanding that, and notwithstanding all the controversy about it, we are asked, on a few words of explanation given in the Railway Committee, to ratify an agreement and deeds, the merits of which we really do not know. I think this is most dangerous
legislation. We may be legislating away valuable rights of some persons without having any knowledge of what we are doing. We certainly do not know the inside of it. I think one of the strong reasons why this House should hesitate to-night ill passing this Bill is that members of the government who were present at the meeting of the Railway Committee entered their strong protest against it and voted to refer the Bill to a sub-committee to examine the deeds. I think that if to-night this House votes this Bill through, it votes condemnation of the government. For, the government has a policy on this Bill, and that policy is that it should not be passed.
I leave that idea in the minds of the supporters of the government, as to whether they are going to condemn the government for having a policy upon a private Bill, which I think it is their duty to have in every instance, because I hold that a government should always have a policy on any legislation passing through this House. They have their law officers, they have their departmental advisers to inform them whether the legislation is proper. No doubt the Department of Railways and Canals had advised the Minister of Railways and Canals in this matter, because he was strongly of the opinion that the Bill should not pass. The hon. member for West Quebec (Hon. Mr. Dobell) took the same stand and opposed the Bill. I believe that these hon. gentlemen knew what they were doing, I believe that they took that ground for good reasons ; and, as I said before, I have no doubt that it is the sentiment of the entire government. I think that the members of this House sitting behind the Treasury benches ought to pause before they pronounce condemnation against the government by supporting a Bill of which they do not know the merits.

I received, and I suppose other gentlemen did also, a printed circular a few days ago, in which the writer protests against the passage of this South Shore Company's Bill. This printed document is signed by J. H. Wood, of 101 Bleury street, Montreal. I do not know who the gentleman is, but he says :
Dear Sir,-On behalf of a number of workingmen, whose claims would be wiped out by the passing of the Act respecting the South Shore Railway Company, now before the House of Commons, I humbly request you to assist us in getting a proper hearing before the Railway Committee of that House.
The company is asking parliament to ratify titles to property which are in dispute in the courts, which ratification would deprive us and a large number of creditors of their rights.
The South Shore Company is the one which figures in the last report of the Auditor General in connection with the Sorel bridge, and its conduct in that transaction certainly; justifies us in asking that its present demands be closely inquired into.	Yours truly,
J.	H. WOOD.
Mr. GEOFFRION

I did not have an opportunity of being present when the Bill was before the committee, or I would have read the letter. I do not know what it is worth, I read it that the members of the House may be placed in possession of the statements made in it.

No doubt there is something in the objection which has been taken, that the document or deed of sale which it is sought to have ratified by this Bill is not incorporated in the Bill, as is the general rule followed by the Railway Committee. This objection was taken, I understand, before the Railway Committee, but was overruled. I think it is proper on this occasion again to support the ruling of the Railway Committee. I do not share the view of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) that if the House passes this Bill it will be voting censure on the government, because it so happens that two members of the government would prefer to follow the rule generally observed in the procedure of the Railway Committee. I may observe to. my hon. friend, however, that the objection which he raises has not the same validity as it would have in a Bill originating in any other province. By the laws of the province of Quebec, deeds of the character of the one which it is sought to have ratified, are called authentic deeds. There is nothing of the *kind, so far as I know, in any of the English provinces which are subjected to the common law. This deed of sale, or what we call an authentic deed, is deposited with the officer who is the custodian of it. A deed of sale is never delivered to the buyer or purchaser, it invariably remains with the proper officer, whether it be the sheriff, or a notary public, or auy other officer of the law, it remains there on record and he can only give copies of it. If a deed of sale is passed in any of the provinces which enjoy the common law, it may be handed over to another party, and you may be able to get it if you know where it is. But if a deed of sale is passed in the province of Quebec, a deed by the sheriff, or merely a warrantee deed, or simply an ordinary deed of sale passed before a notary public, it remains of record in the hands of the officials who received it. The man who has an interest in seeing the deed cannot get the original of it, he can only buy a copy. Therefore, when you say in this Bill, or a similar Bill, that the deed was of such a date, under such and such a number, deposited on record at such an office, you have the description of that deed, and know exactly what you want, especially if the deed is filed at the time, as it was before the Railway Committee. I understand that matter came before the Railway Committee, all the deeds were produced for examination.
I saw none of the deeds.

I understand they were deposited for inspection of the members who wanted to see them, and certainly it would have been extraordinary if they had not been. But they were there, though they were not incorporated in the Bill. But before they could be incorporated in a Bill you w'ould have to satisfy yourselves as to what they are. Anybody can do it simply by applying to the custodian of that deed, the sheriff of the city of Montreal in this case; and therefore tpy hon. friend will see that his objection has not the same weight it would have in reference to a Bill coming from a province subjected to the common law. Therefore, though the deed is not incorporated in that Bill, still it is plain we know exactly what it was. The object of the deed is to ratify a certain number of sheriff's sales which had transferred this railway from what was at one time the Atlantic and Lake Superior and South Shore Railway Company. This railway has had a sad history. It has been in the hands of certain parties who have never operated it, but it has at last found its way into the hands of a very respectable company who, at the present time, is running it and giving satisfaction to everybody. It would be most unfortunate if this Bill were not passed. As to the claims of certain workingmen, this circular has been issued, as I know, but the present company, the South .Shore Railway Company, has nothing at all to do with the claims of these men, it is uot in any way responsible for the claims of these men. If there are any, of which I am not aware, they have been incurred by the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway Company, they must have been incurred at least twelve years ago. No steps have been taken, so far as I know, to recover them since that time. The railway has been sold under the sheriff's authority, and therefore the workingmen, if they have any claim, have not the shadow of a title aga'inst the present ownership. I repeat it would be a calamity if this Bill were not to go through, and if the present proprietors of the road could not have an opportunity of operating it successfully.

In answer to the objection which has been made that the title has not been copied or transcribed entirely in the Bill, I may say this matter was left entirely in the hands of the committee. Here is a letter that was addressed to me, because I was taking an interest in the matter :
Re South Shore Railway Bill. Raymond Prefontaine, K.C., M.P.
Dear Mr. Prefontaine,-I inclose herewith copy of your Bill, as I am printing it. I have agreed upon this form with the Law Clerk of the Senate so as to obviate the necessity for printing the agreements, which is both unnecessarily expensive and cumbrous, but the necessary par-1 ticulars in the deeds are, I think, set out, except the date of registration of the conveyance

from Beauchemiu to the South Shore Railway Company (section 2, paragraph 'b '). This date does not appear on the document, if you have it please send it to me by returning mail, if you have it not, it will probably make little difference. I have taken some considerable trouble in getting the Bill into this shape, and I think you will consider that it is satisfactory.
Faithfully yours,

The deeds were in the hands of the clerk of the Railway Committee, they are still in his hands, and he is the custodian of them, so that, if the deeds are not transcribed entirely, there is, I think, sufficient description given in the Bill to satisfy anybody who may be interested in knowing what they contain. The South Shore Railway Company are not responsible in any way. Besides that, the deeds being in the hands of the Railway Committee, there is nothing to be hidden. They are public documents, registered at the registry offices in the different counties in which this property is situated.
When this Bill was being considered in the Railway Committee, and various questions were being asked regarding it, why were the deeds not produced, if they were there ?
I stated that the deeds were in the hands of the clerk of the committee. They were on the table, and I saw them myself.
Certainly, and we referred to them.

I asked the hon. gentleman for the order of sale from the sheriff, and he said it was there. There were two deeds of sale from the sheriff, and I understood that the authority for the sale would be forthcoming. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he has the authority for the second sale ?

There was no authority given to me for the second sale. The authority was given to the sheriff from .the court. The sheriff acted according to the order of the court, which appears by the documents themselves. It was denied by a certain party, by a party who can deny anything at all, even that the sun Is shining that there was an order of the court. There is not only one order of sale, but two orders of sale, one In September, 1895, and one in July, 1899, so that this cannot be denied in any way. and it has nothing to do with the deeds. This all appears from the deeds of the sheriff.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman why it is. if the deeds were in the possession of the clerk of the Railway Committee, that they are not set out as a schedule to this Bill ?
I have just explained it. I have nothing to do with that

except as regards the letter I got from the law clerk of the Railway Committee, who told me, on the 30th of March, that he had agreed with the law clerk of the Senate about adopting this mode of entering the deeds in the Bill. That is the reason, and the deeds, being in the hands of the clerk of the committee, nobody asked to have them incorporated in the Bill.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax) I do not agree that it is not necessary to have them incorporated in the Bill.

Anyway, we cannot be held responsible for the error or fault that may have been committed by an
employee of this House.

I am not finding fault with the hon. gentleman. I merely desire to express the opinion that when we are confirming a deed in this House we ought to have that deed set out in full as a schedule to the Bill.
These are purely and simply deeds of the sheriff, and the transactions that followed the execution of these deeds.
Only one of them is named as the sheriff's deed.
No, there are two.

So far as appears from the Bill. The other deeds mentioned applied to sales from individuals to the railway companies, or from the railway companies to individuals. The third only is mentioned as being a sheriff's sale.

The sale of the Montreal and Sorel road took place, and the road was acquired by Messrs. Beauchemin, Tourville, Fortier and Leduc, and it was transferred to the South Shore Railway Company. The South Shore Railway Company have asked that this deed shall be ratified. That Is all that they require. The only sale about which there seeims to be a good deal of talk is the last sale of the Great Eastern Railway, which was made by the sheriff of the district of Richelieu. That sale was regularly made. I affirm it, and it was not contested within the six months that it could be contested under the laws of our province, excepting by a party named McNally, who withdrew his aetion, so that the deed is good. I will answer the question of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) about the wages of the labourers. That circular that was sent out pretended to be signed by a man named Wood. I know where it originates. It originates with the same party who sold the railway in 1894, and pocketed $92,000. the same party who has been mentioned in connection with all these transactions. His name is well known all over. Every enterprise with which he has been connected has proved disastrous and a loss to everybody.

In order to create trouble and to prevent tbe South Shore Railway Company, which is a responsible company, from using their property as they have a right to use it, he seeks to put obstacles in their way. At the present time they have sixty miles of railway, with two expensive bridges, and they are constructing another one. They have not mortgaged the road for a single cent yet, but they are on the point of mortgaging it to raise money to continue construction, and it is in order to put the title into such a shape that they may borrow money on this railway that they have been obliged to come before parliament for an extension of the time for the construction of the road. They have asked also that the titles be confirmed so (that there can be no doubt raised by the parties who may be called upon to advance money upon the bonds. Now, as regards the creditors of the Great Eastern Railway Company, or the Atlantic and Montreal, this legislation does not affect their rights in any way at all. They have the Atlantic and Lake Superior, which is at present about 100 miles in length down in the Bay des Chaleurs district. These parties have claimed against the railway company, but they have no right to claim against the South Shore Railway Company, because the South Shore Railway Company acquired these deeds regularly through the sheriff's sales, and in those sales creditors were not defrauded of their rights in any way. These sales were public sales, held publicly, and I was very much surprised to hear the hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Ball) saying that there was anything wrong with the sales. The last sale took place in August, 1899. He was present at the sale, and he bid himself on the property. He did not think it was worth more than $500, because he did not bid more. At the previous sale in 1894, when the purchase price was not paid, the hon. member for Nicolet was present, when there was a bid of $20,000 made, and nobody bid over it. The hon. member for Nicolet did not advance a cent of it in order to help them with the sale in 1894. I advanced myself $1,200 that I have not been recouped for yet. The purchase price of $20,000 was never paid by Mr. Armstrong, so that the property had to be resold on the fo'lle enckere of Mr. Armstrong, and it brought only $500, because the property was not worth more. Nobody would buy it. Nobody would take the property from which the rails had been taken away in former years and employed on another railway, but it was not the South Shore Railway Company which did that. The South Shore Railway Company come here and ask simply for a ratification of certain deeds, which were given openly and in a regular manner, and which are now before the House.

We ask simply the ratification of the deeds. That has been 166
done several times, and it has been lone this session for the Grand Trunk Railway.
Mr. BORDEN Halifax). The ratification of a deed made under judicial sale ?

I am not aware that it is necessary, but it cannot do any harm to have parliament ratify a deed which is considered perfect. We know it is a perfect sale and that a judicial deed is the best that can be got. I do not see any harm for parliament to ratify it.

I do not say that there is any harm. I do not know anything about the merits of the Bill, but if we are dealing by way of confirmation with conveyances of this kind we should at least save the rights of persons who may have claims.
If there are any rights they must be recited in the deed.
The deed is not before us.

The deed was produced in the committee for any one to study it if he chose. The law clerk informed me that it was now customary that these long deeds should not be put in a Bill, but merely the dates and the name of the officer before whom they were made.

I do not deny but that these deeds may have been produced, but we certainly did not scan them closely because a certain number of us did not understand them, as these deeds are in the French language.
Some of them are in English.

I am informed that they were in French. Had they been inserted in the Bill they would have been translated and we could have understood them. It is establishing a very bad custom to allow legislation of this kind to go through the House in this manner.
Was any objection raised in the committee ?
No.
Yes.

If these deeds were in French it would certainly have been more regular if they had been translated. I do not know why they were not, but I suppose the members of the committee were satisfied with the explanations that were given. The Bill seeks the ratification of one judicial sale and two voluntary sales. It would have been more regular if the deed had been inserted in the Bill, but the force of that objection is very much weakened by the explanations given. The first is a deed of sale from the Montreal and Atlantic Railway to Mr. Beauchemin, passed before



Mr. Stewart, N.P., of Richelieu. If this deed had been passed in the province of Ontario It would have been signed by the parties in the presence of a notary public and witnessed, and handed to them. The originals might be destroyed) and we afterwards wanted to incorporate them in this Bill we might not be able to obtain them ; but in the province of (Quebec Mr. Stewart is bound by law to keep a copy in his safe.
We have our registry office in Ontario.

And in addition to that the deed is also registered in Sorel. That deed is perfectly authentic, and in a trial in court you are not bound to bring witnesses to prove it as the signature of the notary is sufficient. You see the difference between the British system of procedure and ours. Though it would be more regular to have the deeds in the Bill it does not seem to be a fatal objection. If the Railway Committee was satisfied that the deed was all right, we should take the opinion of the Railway Committee.

The committee was not satisfied.
Hon. Mr. I-IAGGART. I cannot see where any franchise is conveyed to this company, and I would like to know if it is possible under sheriff's sale to transfer the franchise.

I think it is possible because a sheriff's sale conveys everything that belongs to the person who is divested from his property.. I would not, however, give an opinion at this moment as to whether under such a deed the franchise is transferred.

We are now told that the deeds were before the Railway Committee, but personally I knew nothing about it. I raised the objection that the deed was not in the schedule of the Bill. Several gentlemen gave a history of these transactions, some of which were undoubtedly collusive and others fraudulent. The charter of the road passed from one set of men to another, and the former were cut out from their just and legal rights. Mr. Hogg told the committee that if parliament passed this Bill if would deliberately deprive his clients out of their rights and they had no redress. There is no doubt in the world that some of the transactions in connection with this road were fraudulent. The road was sold in one case for $500, and it was admitted afterwards to be a collusive sale.
I deny that. It has never been attacked before the courts.

It was admitted there was no value given to the road. It was understood that this sale would allow the road to pass in the hands of men who could handle it, but no one will say that the road was not worth more than $500. A motion Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
was made in the committee that this Bill be sent to a sub-committee to inquire into the deeds and into the whole transaction. That motion was made by the Minister of Railways and supported by another minister, but it was voted down and the Bill was forced through, contrary to all precedent in that committee. We are told that the clerk of the committee decided with the clerk of the Senate that these deeds should not be inserted in this Bill. What has the clerk of the committee to do with it ?
The law clerk.

Or the law clerk either. We should follow the principle we have always followed, so that we may deal with the matter intelligently. It was because we could not deal with it intelligently that we asked to have it sent to a sub-committee to report upon it. But that was refused, i nd it was put through in the face of the fact that Mr. Hogg declared that if this legislation went through it would legislate out of existence the rights of his clients.
What was the name of his client ?
It was Mr. Charles Armstrong. Mr. Hogg does not make the law, and it tras not the ease simply because he said so.

I forget the name of thP gentleman Mr. Hogg appeared for. It was not Mr. Armstrong. He did not mention Mr. Armstrong's name ; but he said, ' My clients have claims which are being legislated away if this Bill is allowed to pass.'

I want to make a short answer to the statement which the Prime Minister has made. The labour men I refer to are not the men who worked several years ago, but men who have been working on account of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway on the Nicolet section and the Yamaska section. Two years ago they repaired the road from St. Gregoire to Nicolet, so as to allow the trains to pass through, and they made .foundations at St. Francis, Yamaska and Nicolet.
That wffs during the by-election in 1897.

I know you were there, but you did not see any of the men working. With regard to the hon. member for Mais-soneuve and Terrebonne (Mr. Prefontaine), I would say that I was at the sale when he bought the road for $510. As I said before, it was understood that he could buv it for the costs of the court, and resell it for $70,000.
No.

He was to get $60,000 from Mr. Beauchemin. and $10,000 from the Quebec government, and he drew both the

$00,000 and the $10,000. Now, I want to say that I have no objection to this Bill
passing. Far from that, 1 want it to pass.

X just wish to make this point, that if these deeds are all regular and the titla of this company is indisputable, why should they come to this parliament to get legislation to declare that they are so ? I do not think there is any need to ask us to say that something is right which these gentlemen say is right, when we know nothing about it. It is asking too much of this House ; and I am quite sure that if the Minister of Railways is consulted, he will tell us that it is a very dlangerous precedent to establish.
I beg to call attention to the fact that the time for private Bills has expired.

House again in Committee of Supply.
Steel rails, $160,000.

["Air. Speaker, before the House adjourns, I would like to call the attention of the right hon. Prime Alinister to a letter I received from Halifax this morning, in regard to the visit of their Royal Highnesses the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall. It is as follows :

R.	L. Borden, Esq., M.P.,
Ottawa.
Mayor's Office,
Halifax, N.S., May 11, 1901.
Dear Sir,-There is a rumour here that the government might require their Royal Highnesses the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall and York, when visiting Canada, to make their landing at some port other than Halifax.
The city council have, by resolution, requested me to write to you and explain that any change from the published programme of landing at Halifax when visiting Canada would not meet with the approval of the citizens of Halifax, as we have made an appropriation and are making arrangements for the reception; and hope to have the presence and assistance of representatives of both Dominion and local governments.
Yours truly,"]
Who made that statement ?
The statement was made, when the woollen manufacturers went before the hon. gentleman, that they should not make any fuss about this preference for they were all making money.
Is the hon. gentleman referring to something I said ?
I understood that the hon. gentleman said so.
I did not make any such statement. I have no means of knowing whether they make money or not.

The hon. gentleman has means of knowing. He was here and heard the statement made across the floor-which I do not remember his having taken notice of-by an hon. member that the woollen mills in Peterborough were making money. I say that that is not the case in any one of the woollen mills of this country. The hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Ross)- a gentleman for whom 1 have the greatest respect and who no doubt said what he believed to be the case-replied to me the other day contradicting my statement. No doubt he spoke from information he got, but that information was incorrect, if he were to apply for information again, he would get a different answer. When the 121 per cent preference was given to the British goods, those of us who were largely engaged in the woollen manufacture, and who are perfectly loyal to Great Britain and the idea of British connection, did not take exception to that preference, because we did not then know the full extent of it. But we at once set to work to get all the contracts we could before the Yorkshire manufacturers would have a chance to move in the matter. We filled our mills with orders, and the momentum kept them going nearly two years, but gradually the preference began to tell, and this last year I repeat the woollen mills of this country are absolutely ruined. I say that with a full knowledge of what I am talking about. I handed the hon. the Finance Minister to-day a statement of the affairs of six mills of which I have the honour to he president, showing that four of them have lost heavily and that two are only paying one and a quarter per cent on the capital invested. That is the result of the preferential tariff. And when we find these gentlemen showing such anxiety to protect our steel rail industry against slaughter prices-and that is about the only case in which we have ever heard of their doing anything in the shape of protection-we naturally contrast their policy in this respect with that which they have followed in connection with the woollen industry. They are bringing this thing forward now with as much glee as if it were a new toy, and some wonderful invention which they have just discovered. But they are doing more harm by destroying the investments of millions of dollars iD the woollen mills, than they can ever hope to , offset by this new industry which they are seeking to establish and protect. I felt my-

self impelled in the interest of this woollen industry, in which many gentlemen in this House are interested, in which thousands of workingmen are employed-many of whom are now being compelled to leave this country-to protest against its being subjected to competition and slaughter prices from abroad, which must result in their complete ruin. Many of these workingmen have their own houses, which they have been paying for during many years, and which they will have to sacrifice in order to get money to leave the country and find employment elsewhere. And at the head of this woollen industry are many gentlemen who have stood by the party opposite during the eighteen years they were in opposition, relying on the pledge of the party that if returned to power they would give us the entry into a market of 70,000,000 people south of the line. Now, when they find that they cannot succeed in doing that, the least they could do would be to give to this industry, which was built up under the national policy, that these hon. gentlemen now pose as being great supporters of, the same consideration as they are showing the steel works. With regard to the statement which I made a short time ago as to what the hon. Finance Minister said, I was not present at the meeting, but the gentlemen, Mr. Russell and others, who waited on the Finance Minister, told me that they gave him to understand exactly what position the mills were in, and I hope that these hon. gentlemen, In their new found zeal for the policy of protection, will give a little of their consideration to the woollen factories scattered throughout this land; and if they find that I am not exaggerating in any way, I hope they will recognize the great necessity that exists for their doing something to prevent the ruin of this industry and revising their mistaken policy.

If I understood the rigli t hon. gentleman rightly he spoke of a member of this House posing as a minister of the Crown. I do not think that such a statement should be allowed to go unnoticed. There is no man here in any capacity except as an ordinary member of parliament.

I hope the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) will take notice and govern himself accordingly. When I entered the House a moment ago, my hon. friend was referring, not to what somebody else had said, but to what I had said. His statement was that I had said that the woollen mills were making money. I never made any statement as to whether the mills were making money or not. I have no desire, on the question before the House, to be drawn into a general discussion on the woollen tariff. Lest, however, the tears my hon. friend has shed may mislead anybody,

it may be well to mention that the woollen maustry has still 23A per cent protection and free wool. If we are going to weep let us understand what we are weeping about. It would hardly be appropriate to weep over the ruin of an industry because of want of protection, when it enjoys a very liberal protection-when the wooi it imports is free, and it has 234 per cent protection against Great Britain and 35 per cent against the rest of the world.

I have stated that a large quantity of the goods come in from Germany to England where 25 per cent of labour is done on them, and they are then brought into this country, under the preferential tariff, although to the extent of 75 per cent they are German manufacture.

The hon gentleman thinks that that is an argument in his favour. I happen to have in my hand an extract from the London correspondent of the Montreal Gazette. That is pretty good authority. That the correspondent says referring to some opinions expressed in this House :
The idea that foreign goods are finding their way to Canada via England and thus evading the tariff on foreign imports is not generally entertained by traders here. Even if merchants' firms would lend themselves to a fraud which must greatly prejudice the interests of British trade, it is not supposed it is done to any appreciable extent, for the simple reason that the Canadian importer as a rule buys, not from the merchant or the commission agent, on whom suspicion now rests, but direct from the British manufacturer. The commission merchant houses here which trade with the Cape and Australia and India, are mostly all of enormous wealth and of high reputation, and their own interests Closely allied to the interests of the British manufacturers, that they are above suspicion of any unfair trading, and if they are now doing a little business with Canada, It may be safely assumed they have no interest or wish to cheat the government which has alone in our colonies given us a preferential tariff. It is confidently believed here by business men that no proof of frauds to any extent will be forthcoming.
Wait until fraud is charged. They come in under the law. They have 25 per cent of the work done in England, but the goods are 75 per cent German goods, and they still come in legally.
My hon. friend will not be strictly accurate. Seventy-per cent may not be German goods, for the wool may have come from Australia, which Is a British colony.
Does it come free into Germany ?
I could hardly answer my hon. friend off-hand, but I should think not, for Germany is a protective country. But that makes no difference.

It makes a great difference. You are making a great to-do about wool coming in here free. But if the Germans can import the wool and pay duty, manufacture the goods and send them to England, they are doing better.

I do not wish to pose as one giving judgment on the woollen industry question. But I think that an industry that has its wool free and has a protection of 234 per cent against Great Britain, and 35 per cent against the rest of the world, cannot be suffering as severely as some hon. gentlemen think.
But the facts speak louder than the hon. gentleman's theory.

My hon. friend was good enough to send me some papers which I have not had time to read, but which I shall read, and for which I am obliged to him. I regret that he made the statement that the woollen mills in Canada have been ruined. I regret it, because they are not all so fortunate as to have gentlemen at their backs like the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock); and the statement from him that every woollen mill is in a ruinous condition may help to ruin some of the smaller ones.
You need never be afraid of the truth. I am not afraid of it.

My observation of my hon. friend leads me to believe that he does not deal in it more largely than his neighbours. He is subject to all the weaknesses of the other members of the House, and may occasionally make some mistake, mistakes which ungenerous people might say were not wholly excusable. For instance I heard him say that the Minister of Customs iHon. Mr. Paterson) had made statements which he must have known that were not true.
Certainly.

That is
a very ungenerous thing.
As Minister of Customs.

I do not know any standard of truth which would justify a man in saying one thing as a member of the House and another thing as Minister of Customs. My hon. friend may make that distinction ; but we on this side, in our simplicity, do not draw such distinctions. An untruth is an untruth whether it is told by a member of parliament or by the Minister of Customs. My hon. friend refers to a statement made by the Minister of Customs that these rails were being purchased and this industry was being established in Canada without any cost to the country other than paying a

fair price for the rails. My hon. friend took exception to that. He said they are paying a bounty. X suppose he was surprised to discover that there was no bounty on rails at all. Now, he says

I am astonished that the hon. gentleman would attempt to beg off in such a way as that, by saying that steel rails have no bounty. You cannot make steel rails without iron, and iron that has been converted into steel billets, on both of which there is a bounty. The Minister of Finance might as well not attempt anything of that kind.

But if I were to say that the wool and the cloth that is made'from it are the same my hon. friend would insist that there is a difference. He says that the steel rail and the iron are allee samee anyhow, but when you come to woollens and woollen clothing, they are not allee samee anyhow. There is no bounty on steel rails. It does not follow that because a man makes steel rails he gets a bounty on the iron or on the steel. He may buy the pig iron and convert it into steel, or he may go further and buy the steel ingots and convert them into steel rails, and may not get a copper of bounty.
But Mr. Clergue in his speech said differently. He acknowledged that they were receiving a bounty of $7 a ton.

If Mr. Clergue makes pig iron, he will get a bounty: if he makes steel ingots he will get a bounty, but if he makes steel rails he will get no further bounty. My hon. friend from Centre Toronto would not take a position against the encouragement of home industry ; he would not take a position against the bounty, but says that if the bounties are not enough we should give more. Now, if Mr. Clergue will take ore and make it into pig iron he will get a bounty, and my hon. friend says that is all right. If Mr. Clergue or anybody else will make steel and ship it to any point in the wide world he will get a bounty, and that is all right. But if he takes the steel into a factory and makes steel rails thus employing Canadian labour, then the hon. member for Centre Toronto would say that is all wrong. He would stand by the making of the iron, and he would stand by the making of the steel, and would raise no question of the cost; but the moment you go a step further and propose the manufacture of steel rails, he objects on the ground that it will involve large cost to the country. As I have pointed out. the making of steel rails has nothing to do with the bounty at all. This steel rail question must stand upon its own merits ; there is no reason why it should be confused with any other question. It is quite feasible to divide the in-Mr. FIELDING.
dustry-one man may make the iron and steel, and another man may make the steel rails.
Will the hon. minister allow me to ask him a question ?
Certainly.

If by reason of an immense export trade in steel rails the consumption of steel were increased one-half, would not the hon. gentleman say that there was a tax upon Canada by reason of the steel rails ?

I do
not quite see the point.

Perhaps I have not made myself quite clear. The hon. minister is drawing a fine distinction between the steel and the rails, and says that the bounty on the steel has nothing to do with the rails. Does he go that far ?

For the
purpose of this discussion that has nothing to do with it.

But I am speaking for the purposes of fact. As a fact, if we increase our export trade to a large extent and thus consume all the iron and steel made in Canada in the production of steel rails, could it be said that steel rails have nothing to do with increasing the taxes?
I do not see why the hon. gentleman should draw the line at steel rails. It would be the same if the manufacture were carried further, and the material were made into watch springs.

Let me ask my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) a question. What is the object of the bounty given to the manufacture of iron and steel ? Is it not for the purpose of stimulating and enlarging the industries of Canada connected with the production or these articles, to the fullest extent ? But my hon. friend, who is heartily in sympathy with the idea of a bounty upon iron and steel, holds up both hands and says he is prepared to treat such industries in the most liberal manner.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Quite so.
Is the hon. gentleman prepared to put a limit upon the extent to whicn that industry ought to go, and to say, if you enlarge it beyond a certain point it is going to be an injury to Canada ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No.

That is the result of ihe hon. gentleman's argument, and I Will show him

why, if he will open his mind to reason. If the hon. gentleman admits that the production of steel rails is going to cause a greater production of steel and iron in Canada, and therefore to increase the amount the people will he called upon to pay in bounty, if that occurs, then an injury is going to be done to the Canadian people. That is the argument the hon. gentleman is making. In other words, if he is to be consistent in his advocacy of a bounty given for the purpose of increasing to the utmost extent the production of steel and iron in Canada, he would hail with satisfaction the production of any allied industry which would increase the production of iron and steel in the country. Instead of that he says, No. He is crying out against steel rails being made in Canada, because, as he says, we are going to increase the bounty. Ami why are we going to increase the bounty ? Because we are going to increase the amount of iron and steel which is going to be produced and required for manufacturing purposes in Canada.
Now, the argument has been made by the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Hr. Brock), and I think it has been made by other gentlemen in this House, that we are paying $7 more for these steel rails than we would pay if the bounty were not given, because we are entitled to add to the cost of the rails the amount of the bounty. Now, I would ask my hon. friend to reconcile such a statement as that with the argument that hon. gentlemen opposite have been making since the commencement of this discussion. Their contention has been that you must make your contracts with the Sault Ste. Marie company so rigid as to insist upon the manufacture and production of these steel rails altogether in Canada. That is the argument. You must not have these steel rails partially made in Canada, you must not ask the neighbouring country to send into Canada material for simply rolling the rails, you must have them all made in Canada. What is the result of making them all in Canada ? The result is that you have to pay bounty upon the product, you have to pay bounty upon your iron and steel that enter into the finished rails. My hon. friend complains in one breath that you have not made your contract rigid enough, and that all you want is a guarantee that these things are going to be done in Canada from beginning to end ; and in the next breath he says you ought not to do this, because you are going to add the price of the bounty to the rails. That is the argument he has made. He is on the horns of a dilemma and he cannot get out of it. I think it is the funniest position I ever heard taken by a business man in any deliberative assembly, is this position taken by the member fov Centre Toronto, that you are entitled to add the amount of the bounty to the price of the steel rails.
Now where is the justification of the argument that there is a shadow of protection
in the policy of this government ? Where do you find it? Examine this transaction as closely as you may, and you will not find the shadow of a shade of protection in it. Do we put a tariff upon rails imported by this arrangement and in pursuance of this policy ? No. How then are you going to say there is a shadow of protection in the transaction unless you are going to put a tariff upon the importation of steel rails into Canada ? Or, if you like to extend the idea -and it is hardly open to such an extension -unless you put the bounty upon steel rails. But it is neither. There is no tariff against the importation of rails into Canada, and there is no bounty upon the production of steel rails, not one farthing. Where then do you find the protection ? You will search in vain to find the shadow of protection in this transaction. Look at it fairly, look at it as men whose minds are open to reason, and you will not find the idea of protection. We do not say to Mr. Clergue, or the Lake Superior Power Company that we will give them any advantage, that we will give them any preference further than this, that we engage to buy from them 25,000 tons of rails a year at the price that governs in the open market in Great Britain. Now if the hon. gentlemen opposite did not have any more protection in their policy from the moment that the great national policy was established down to the present time, they would not have much to boast of in the 'way of protection, and we would not have much to condemn. This is a fair, open transaction, giving to our own people simply the preference to which I think they are reasonably entitled, saying to them : Make rails for us at the prices of the open market in London, we won't go across the water, we won't go across the line, we won't go outside our own country, we will, go to you and give you the same money we would give to anybody else. Yet, hon. gentlemen opposite [DOT].pretend to discover in that transaction a big mountain of protection.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. gentleman is reading a lecture now to the Minister of Finance when he declares that this is no protection. Is he falsifying the words of the Minister of Finance who declared that this was a measure of protection to compensate the manufacturers of iron for protection by way of customs duties taken away ?
Are you talking of this contract ?

No, but what is infinitely of greater importance, the broad principle upon which bounties were paid. Now I want to say to the hon. gentleman that when these bounties were increased it was with the assent of both sides of this House. It is a measure of protection. I will put the two sides of the question : We are giving a large amount of protection by way of ad-

vantage, because protection after all is the advantage the manufacturer has in Canada over the manufacturer of a foreign country. I will put the one case of bounties paid upon the products of the Canadian manufacturer as a protection, and I will put the other case of high import duties as a protection. Now what do they mean ? In the one case it would mean that the foreign manufacturer would have to pay duties to get in here. But in the other case it would mean that the people of Canada, under a system of bounties, paid the compensation to the manufacturer here who had the advantage. If he gave a high measure of protection by customs duty would he exclude competition ? Would he say we were bound first to protect the manufacturer V Under a customs duty we are bound to shut out competition. I have no hesitation in declaring that on general principles bounties are unsound and indefensible. Bounties are not paid by the foreign competitors, as they may be under customs duties.
The hon. gentleman is in favour of it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do favour it. I say that the general proposition is indefensible ; but, I say that in this particular case it would be justifiable : yet, the hon. gentleman reiterates the. statement that we are opposed to bounties. No, we favour bounties, but we do not favour bounties, and at the same time exclude the persons who receive these bounties from the measure of competition that they are entitled to in this country. It would make no difference whether it was customs duties that gave the manufacturer the advantage or whether it was a bounty paid out of the pockets of the people of the country. AYhat we are complaining of. is that you have shut out competition besides. Now, the hon. gentleman is endeavouring to make a distinction between iron and steel rails. There is absolutely no distinction. If you can turn all the iron into steel rails that is made in Canada, first into pig and then into steel billets and in this way turn it all into steel rails, will the hon. gentleman pretend to say that that would not be a tax on the people of a direct class ? I say it is a tax of a most unmistakable character upon the people. I say at the same time that it is a tax that is to be justified. I do not wish the hon. gentleman to torture it into the shape that he is attempting to do. I concluded from the poverty of his argument that he was forced to make the statement that we were opposed to it or that our arguments were susceptible of such a construction. It is clear that we still favour it. We think it is the duty of the government to carry out the contract that was made by reason of an Act passed in this House, which constitutes an act of good faith. The government would not be justified in refusing to do this. They must carry that out, but our Mr. CLANCY.
complaint is that this bounty is a tax upon the people, as the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) has stated, and that the manufacturer should not be freed from competition in addition to that. There is no doubt about that. It is never paid by the foreigner, even by accident, tt is paid out of the public purse. I say that it can only be justified on special grounds. I believe I think it is a justifiable measure of protection, or advantage, or whatever you may call it, to the manufacturers. The hon. Minister of Finance says that it is to compensate the manufacturers for the protection we are taking away. It is on the iron from which the steel rails are made and it does not make any difference. If the steel rails had to be made before the pig iron was made. I could understand the hon. gentleman's argument, but unfortunately for the pursuit of an argument of that kind, the material out of which the steel rails are to be made has to receive the bounty in a direct way. I do not think it is worth while pursuing the argument a single moment. It is a direct tax upon the people. I say it is a justifiable tax under the circumstances. I think the hon. gentlemen are not strengthening their case by taking that position, but the difficulty is that while we want to deal fairly with the manufacturers of the country, as we ought to do, the hon. gentlemen are now dealing unfairly with the taxpayer of the country, who has to pay that tax, and I repeat, a justifiable tax, but it is not justifiable, if you ask him to pay without the advantage of competition. The hon. gentlemen are giving this company an advantage in Canada, but they are preventing healthy competition in our own country, that friendly, thrifty strife, that always gives tone to business. Competition is withered by the course that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has pursued. The hon. gentleman need not imagine that by his clever system of dust-throwing he can deceive the people of the country.

Mr. Chairman, there have been new doctrines of political economy laid down this evening that I have never heard before. I heard the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) make the solemn statement in his strident tones that the new system of paying bounties is not one of protection. I have always understood from the authorities on political economy that it is the most offensive system of protection, the most aggressive system of protection. The Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) made a statement, the most extraordinary I have ever heard, in which he said that the government had established this industry without it costing the counti'y a cent. If I understood the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals rightly, he said that there were fine mines of ore on the north shore, containing a small portion of nickel and that he was going to get a superior kind

of rail out of that ore, that he was going to establish, not only the mining of ores on the north shore of Lake Superior, hut that he was going to establish an industry at Sault Ste. Marie for the purpose of converting the ore into blooms of steel and then into steel rails. I thought perhaps that he had made provision in his contract for all that, but, when I came to read the contract,
I found, strange to say, that these rails may be manufactured out of ore that is mined in any part of the world. The hon. minister led the committee to believe that we were going to establish not only the mining industry on the north shore of Lake Superior, but that we were going to establish a pig iron industry where blooms of steel were to be manufactured, but it turns out that under the conditions that Mr. Cler-gue has made in the contract he does not need to have the ore mined in Canada. All he has to do is to make the blooms of steel from which the rails are manufactured in Canada. So that, we are not to have a smelting industry after all, to be established at Sault Ste. Marie, but we are only going to have manufactured in this country the blooms of steel and the rails. What becomes of that part of the argument which the bon. Minister of Railways and Canals made in reference to the mining ores and the establishing of pig iron furnaces in the country ? Why does he not answer that, after saying that by the contract which he has made with Mr. Clergue he is going to establish this industry and thereby going to confer a great benefit upon the country ? There is not a word of it in the contract ? In the contract there is a stipulation that the blooms of steel shall be manufactured in the country from which the steel rails are made. Then, the iron ores may come from any part of Lake Superior, or they may come from the American side, the pig iron may be taken from any part of the United States if it is found cheaper, and there is no industry of that kind dependent upon the contract made between the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals and this gentleman who is to furnish steel rails. Then, I would ask the hon. minister if he would point out to us what is to become of the magnificent ore beds they have on the north shore of Lake Superior, from the ore of which would be manufactured a superior kind of pig iron, from which the blooms of steel are manufactured, and which, after being manufactured, will contain 2 or it per cent of nickel, when we are only to have rolling mills at Sault Ste. Marie and make blooms of steel manufactured from material which may be obtained in any part of the world ?
That being the case, the hon. gentleman will be in a position to reassure those alarmed associates of his, as to the cost of the rails, and the bounty which will be paid.
speakername: Teh MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Not only will there be no bounty, but we will get $2.50 a ton duty on the pig iron.

These hon. gentlemen opposite all along left the House under the impression that the bounty would be paid to the manufacturers of these rails, but we find now that that is not the case. The House has been misled. Every person believed that this contract was for the purpose of establishing a steel rail industry in Canada, the ore to be mined here, the blooms to be made here, and all this was to be fostered by that contract for 125,000 tons of rails. But now we find the contract is so varied from the statement of the hon. minister (Mr. Blair) that one-half of the work may be done in a foreign country, that we are" to have no mines worked, no smelting furnaces worked, and nothing but a rolling mill after all. Why did not the Minister of Railways tell the House that, and take us into his confidence as he should have done ? Did the Minister of Finance know that this pig iron would be manufactured in a foreign country ? I doubt it.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE!' I did. I was wondering where we were going to pay the bounty on that.
And you were talking all the time about $6 a ton bounty ?
1 was comforting myself with the thought that on every ton of that pig iron we would get $2.50 duty, instead of paying a bounty, so that whatever side you look at it we stood to win.

Then, the starting of this industry under this paternal government has vanished into the misty air. Let the House know that all we are going to have under this contract is a rolling mill at the ' Soo.' There is not a single man in this
the processes to the finished product of Canadian steel rails. Would the minister now explain why it was he purchased a large quantity of coal for the Intercolonial Railway, and how much he paid for it ? Our railway runs quite close to the mines in Cape Breton, and there must have been some reason for purchasing large quantities of coal in the United States. I have heard no explanation of it yet.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND
CANALS. The reason why my hon. friend has had no explanation of it is. because he never mentioned the matter until now. It is quite true that some time ago it was found necessary to purchase coal in the United States. I suppose that no one imagines for a moment that we would voluntarily go

for coal to a foreign country instead of purchasing it along the line of our own railway, but the facts are these. The employees in the mines of Nova Scotia were organizing for a strike, and had about completed their arrangements to do so. The general manager of the Intercolonial Railway telegraphed me that the conditions were very critical, and that on account of the extreme prdsperity of the coal business, and the enormous demands for coal, the Intercolonial Railway had not been able to get from the Canadian collieries as large a supply as they desired. When that strike was threatened, there were important points on the road at which we had only one day's supply of coal, and there was no place from one end of the line to the other where we had more than two or three days' supply. Every one will admit that under such circumstances the government could only acquit itself of its responsibility by securing a supply of coal wherever it could be obtained. in view of the possibility of our supply being cut off from the Canadian collieries. Acting upon the advice, the very urgent advice, of the officers who have charge of this department, I authorized them to procure enough coal to answer for present needs, getting no more than would be absolutely required, until we knew the result of the threatened proceedings ; and some
55,000	tons were obtained. Our consumption is 400,000 tons for the year, so that lion, gentlemen can see that 55,000 tons would not furnish us with a very large store to cover any lengthened period of strike ; and it was above all things the bounden duty of those who were charged with the responsibility to see that the railway was supplied with sufficient coal to keep the railway in operation during the threatened strike.
What price was paid ?

I cannot say the exact price, but it was about the same as the coal costs us from the collieries of our own country. There may be 10 cents or 15 cents difference one way or the other ; but. we got it from various parties in competition as well as we could, and at the best market prices. I do not know from whom the coal was obtained.
I think $3.30 was the price we paid the home collieries for coal delivered on our own line.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Where was the American coal delivered ?
We got the coal in the United States at very much less than that-$2.50, $2.60. or $2.75, paying the freight, which would bring it up to. perhaps, $3.50.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman say from what company he got the coal, and at what period ?
I cannot say. We got it in small quantities from different people, and had it brought to different points.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: At what period was it the minister made the discovery about this strike being imminent ?
I cannot name the day. I think it was a matter of public observation. It was reported in the newspapers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Can he tell the month ?
I think it would be before Christmas, but I am not sure. My deputy tells me it was before Christmas.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the minister tell the committee whether he communicated with the managers of the different mines as to their ability to supply the coal ?

I communicated with nobody but the general superintendent. I took his advice and acted upon it. I authorized him to act upon his judgment if the occasion was critical and a strike appeared to be imminent.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The managers of the mines would be in a better position to give information as to the probability of a strike than any one else. The hon. gentleman justifies the purchase in the United States on the ground of the imminence of a strike. It seems to me that he was derelict in his duty in not communicating with the managers of the mines in Nova Scotia, and ascertaining what they had to say on the subject. I have information which I may state to the hon. gentleman, that if he had communicated with the managers of some of those mines, he would have found that there was no great probability of a strike being allowed to prevail. as the men would have been arranged with or their demands conceded rather than that a strike should be permitted to go on.
I may tell him that there is a good deal of dissatisfaction on the part of his own friends in the province of Nova Scotia in regard to this matter.
I cannot help that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not say that the hon. gentleman can help it, but I give him that information for his soul's health, so that he may avoid making a similar mistake in the future.
I would do exactly the same thing again.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Here is an article from the Mining Record, which is edited by a very prominent Liberal in the

province of Nova Scotia-if I am not mistaken-tlie Hon. Robert Drummond, a member of tbe legislative council of Nova Scotia. This is what he says about it :
We have disquieting news as to the condition of the coal trade. The boom, if our information is correct, is to be of shorter duration than most people expected. It is asserted chat the folly of the Minister of Railways in ordering coal from the United States is partly responsible for this. The coal companies cannot get cars, and the consequence is that coal is coming into Montreal from the United States. Coal from the United States, and even from Scotland, is selling at about $4 per ton. The Drummond colliery will go on half-time this week, as cars cannot be obtained to keep the pit going. This is certainly a rather serious and startling state of affairs.
What is the date of that ?

The 3rd day of April, 1901. I do think it would have been only ordinary prudence on the part of the hon. gentleman to have communicated with the managers of those mines, because it is perfectly clear that they would _ know a great deal more about the probability of a strike being allowed to proceed than could the hon. gentleman or any of his officers.

I desire to say just one or two words in reply to what the hon. leader of the opposition says in regard to the threatened strike in the province of Nova Scotia. I have no knowledge whatever of what the situation was m the mines of Nova Scotia proper, in the counties of Cumberland and Rictnu ; but,
I do know, from personal knowledge, that the managers of the Dominion Coal Company expected a strike. The men served the managers with notices that on a certain day they would strike, and it was within a few days of the expiration of the time that a settlement was reached and a strike averted, the companies consenting to arbitrate the difficulties between them and the miners. I am perfectly certain that if the Minister of Railways had consulted the manager of the Domnion Coal Company within two days of the settlement, his reply would have been that he expected a strike. I consulted 'several of the men at the head of affairs in the county of Cape Breton, and I know, as a matter of fact, that they expected a strike.

I, of course, anticipated and expected criticism for the course I have taken: but, I would very much prefer to bear all the criticism that may be incident to my having authorized my officers to exercise their judgment and procure the coal, than to lay myself open to the charge of having, in the face of a threatened strike, failed to take the necessary steps in order that the Intercolonial Railway should not be closed down.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I adhere exactly to what I said before, that I think it was the duty of the hon. gentleman to communicate with the mining managers before adopting this course. They are the people who would know whether or not they would make concessions which would prevent a strike from taking place. It may be true that my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) had some special knowledge about this. But, he was not the Minister of Railways and Canals. If the Minister of Railways had made himself acquainted with tlie facts, which the hon. member for Cape Breton, brings to the attention of the House, the criticism I have offered to-night *would not have been made. The point I am making is, that the Minister of Railways should have consulted these mme managers and taken the best possible means of information before taking the extreme step of going to the United States to buy coal.

No doubt I would rather see all the coal required for the Intercolonial, as well as for all the people of Canada, bought in Canada. But I submit that the leader of the opposition has missed the point he was trying to make. Does he not think that Mr. Pottinger did make these inquiries ?
The Minister of Railways says he did not.

No, he says that he himself did not. I know that there was continual communication going on. I know that two days before the strike, a large mine owner told Mr. Pottinger that it was impossible the strike could be averted, because the owners would not yield to the miner's demands.
I asked the hon. minister if he had communicated with these mine managers and he said not.
Not personally.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I did not expect that the minister would write every letter with his own hand and communicate with the mine managers himself personally. He cannot do everything, but I supposed he understood me to mean by himself or his officers.

The hon. gentleman asked me if I had communicated with the mine managers and I said I had not. I was satisfied that we could not do otherwise than we did. In the first communication which I received from the general superin tendent, he assured me that a strike was imminent and advised me, in the strongest possible terms, to make arrangements as speedily as possible to secure a supply of ccal. I could not, iu the face of tlie warning, refuse to make such arrangements. If

I had, the hon. gentleman, instead of corn-plaining now about my getting the coal in the united States, would have said : Were you not advised by your superintendent, who was on the ground, and who knew what was happening, to get your coal elsewhere ? Why did you not do so ? I very much prefer being criticised from the other point of view under the circumstances.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Does the hon. the leader of the opposition think that the manager of a coal mine would tell the minister directly or even the superintendent of the IntercoV onial, whether there was to be a strike or not :	That might come to the ears of the
men, and if the men knew that the manager said there was to be a strike, they would say he is expecting it, and would go' on with it. And if they knew that he said there was not going to be a strike, they would conclude that they were going to get what they wanted. 1 do not know that after all the strike was an uninixed evil. I think it taught a lesson botli to the mine-owners and the men, which will make them more particular about a strike then they were before. Once they know that the' best cusr tomer they have, the Intercolonial Railway, is not going to lie caught napping, and that it will get its coal elsewhere, they will be a little more particular than they are sometimes, although i am bound to say that the men are not more unreasonable than those who employ them. But the fullest information we had from conversations with the men and others, and that is the only way you could get information. You could never get directly from the managers as to whether or not there would be a strike, and the information directly from the workingmen themselves would not be very reliable No man of sense would, under the circumstances have done otherwise than bring in coal from the outside, because if the Intercolonial Railway were to stop running only one day that would be a most serious matter, far worse than the obtaining of our coal elsewhere and not losing anything by the transaction.

and give them the advance in wages they asked. It will be refreshing to the labouring classes in Nova Scotia to learn that the hon. member for Guysborough was not the champion of the workingmen, but was afraid that they would succeed in getting their advance, and therefore he folded his arms and stood idly by so that they might be defeated in their object. Whether the men were right or not in their demands, I do not know, but I know that in the hon. gentleman they had no friend.

Whether the men were right or wrong, the hon. gentleman thinks we should have stood by them, and says that by not giving this contract we prevented their getting tlieir advance. But there was no contract pending then between the government and the coal company. These contracts are made at the beginning of the season; and if there had been a strike and the company had not come to a settlement with the men, the Intercolonial Railway would have been without supplies. The minister, therefore, had the best possible reason for getting his supply elsewhere. There was no contract pending, and if the company had paid higher wages^ that would not have affected the price paid by the government, because the government had a contract for the season.

Then the position is this. If the Intercolonial Railway or the government had entered into a contract with the mine-owners, the mine-owners would have been obliged to carry out the contract to the letter. If they did not, they would render themselves amenable to damages.
If there was a strike, you could not compel the company to deliver the coal.
Does the hon. gentleman ask the House to believe that every contract made includes a clause that if a strike happened the contract is off ?
The hon. gentleman should understand that if a strike is on, the company cannot deliver the coal, and the government could not run the railway without it.

If they did not deliver the coal, they would subject themselves to damages, and they would therefore see the necessity of guarding against a claim for damages by acceding to the wishes of the men.
Mi'. FRASER. Not necessarily.
Why not.

It might be that the company would consider it better to pay the damages than increase the wages, because the government could get nothing except the difference between what they would have to pay elsewhere for coal and their contract price with the mine-owners.

The government then would he In this position, that they could recover the penalty and get their coal elsewhere. The hon. member for Guysborough has rather been touched on the raw, posing, as he always does, as a friend of labour. From this out he will be regarded as the very opposite.

If the hon. gentleman thinks that his opinion has weight with this committee or the people he is very much mistaken. If he thinks that to descend to small personal criticism in conducting a debate is going to benefit himself or injure anybody, he is mistaken. This House is beyond that. What this government did is what would have been done by any competent administrator. I did not say the men were right in their strike. It was not the question whether they were right or wrong. But I say the managers are as often wrong as the workmen. The workmen are not always wrong. I have never said and I will not say now, that if the workmen are wrong we must stand by them as against the managers. The hon. gentleman is welcome to any little gain he can make from his attempt at humour.
