I do not think that all the facts in this case have been brought out. As a matter of fact there was a strike on in the mines of the Acadia Coal Company and the Drummond mine, in Pictou County.
When was that ?
At the time the contract was made.
But at what time ?

I do not remember the exact date, but I remember the circumstances. Now, I do not agree with all that has been said on this side, but I rather agree with the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax). Before making this American contract, they should have consulted with the managers. I do not blame the minister, for he was depending on a report from his officers in Moncton, I believe. But the officers became hysterical and advised him wrongly. I do not believe the strike was as imminent as they thought it was. They took their information from the statement given out in Montreal. The mine managers met in Montreal to consider the demands of the men, and the statement was given out to the press-they deny that it was given out officially-that the managers had concluded unanimously to resist the men's demands. On that statement, the officials of the Intercolonial Railway advised the minister that a strike was imminent, and this large quantity of coal was ordered.
I do not think that we could quarrel with the Department of Railways, if, under these circumstances they had ordered 15,000 or
20,000	tons to tide them over a week or two. But I do say-and I regret to say it as
a supporter of the government-that the officials of the Intercolonial Railway made a mistake in ordering such a large quantity of coal from American collieries to be brought into Canada. It should be our first policy to give work to the men of Canada. The same principle applies here as in the Clergue contract. Every inquiry should be made before the government make the contract with a foreign corporation in competition with the coal miners of Nova Scotia. So far as the colliery at Spring Hill was concerned, there was no strike, there was a threatened strike. The manager was in Montreal with the others. The statement was made in the newspapers that the management would resist the demands of the men and it was said that a strike would follow. But when a strike threatened, before the government go so far as to order) coal from the United States collieries, they ought to make themselves sure to a certainty that there is going to be a strike and that coal cannot be got from Canadian coal mines.
I would ask the Minister of Finance what is the beginning of the season of which he speaks when he says that at that time these contracts were made?

I would rather that the Minister of Railways were here to answer that question. But my recollection is that, in the early summer, they make contracts covering the whole period.
I think that, usually, during the session of parliament the matter is discussed with the coal companies and that after the end of the session is about the time for making the contracts.

As I understood the minister he anticipated bitter criticism of this purchase of coal from the United States. 5Tet he finds fault because we ask how many tons were bought, what the prices were, from whom the coal was purchased and other perfectly fair questions on that line. Anticipating keen criticism he should have charged his memory with all the facts regarding this matter. We are justified in offering the criticism we have, because the minister has declined to furnish us with reasonable information. No one would attempt to say that $180,000 worth of coal brought into this country is not of sufficient importance to arouse inquiry. We find hon. gentlemen on the other side differing somewhat upon the subject of the strike. We find one hon. gentleman saying that the officials were in a hysterical state of mind
The railway officials.

I understand. We find the Minister of Railways admitting that there was only two days' supply of coal. If that is the case, it strikes me that the officials were very much to blame-to have only two days' supply of coal in the face of a threatened strike. I think the minister ought to be prepared with reasonable information so

that we may understand exactly the state of the case.	*

I think the hon. gentleman's questions with regard to the price of coal, from whom purchased and the quantity, were quite proper, and if the hon. Minister of Railways had been here I am sure he would he glad to say that the information would be brought down. The minister had to leave and our purpose was to turn to another branch of the estimates. But if it is desired to continue this discussion, we have no wish to stop it.

I wish to say a word before this subject is dropped. Before the Minister of Railways went away, we tried to get from him this information which the Minister of Finance admits it is quite proper that we should have. As the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) pointed out, the hon. minister said that he expected the severest criticism of his acts. If he did, he should have come down to the House with exact and positive information so as to be able to defend the course of his department. Now, we have tried to ascertain the day of this purchase. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) was unable to give it. Perhaps the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) could tell us.
I could not give the exact date.
Well, within a week or two.
1 think it was in the month of December, but I am not sure
I cannot give 'the day of the month, but I think it was about the next day after the statement made in Montreal newspapers that the managers intended to stand against the demands of the men.
That is not very definite.
Was it before or after the election ?
After.

In reply to the hon. member, I might point out that the hon. minister said that the reason why he had not this information was that he has not been asked. If notice had been given he would have had the information.

Another extraordinary thing about it is that the hon. minister told us that the case was so very urgent that he was in communication with the general manager and that he at once authorized him to secure the coal in the United States without-as has been very properly pointed out by the leader of the opposition and the hon. member from Cumberland-without finding out, as he should have done, whether the strike was likely to occur, and, if it did occur, what amount of coal could be furnished by the colliery companies.

Surely, they can supply a certain quantity. The minister told us to-night that in important places there was only one day's supply of coal, and at many other important points there were only twp or three days' supply of coal. Can you imagine, Mr. Chairman, a business concern, run on business principles, by great business men, as they claim to be, coming to the House with such a declaration as that ? Why, they only have an average of two days' supply of coal for the running of the Intercolonial Railway. I venture to say that if they go to the Grand Trunk coal piles, if they go to the Canadian Pacific coal heaps, they will find that weeks' and months' supply is always kept on hand, 1 venture to say that you cannot go to Toronto Junction any day in the twelve months, when you will not find tens of thousands of tons in one big heap, for the supply of the Canadian Pacific Railway, or a small section of their line, because these dumps are in all parts of the system. But here is a railway being run with two days' supply of coal. I never heard of such magnificent management of a railway before. And they spend $192,000 of Canadian money to buy coal in the United States, when that coal could be promptly supplied in Canada. The minister was not able to tell us in the first place whether there was likely to be a strike, and in the second place, whether he had asked the companies how much coal they could supply right away. The minister does not tell us that he made such inquiries at all. The member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) says that the general manager was hysterical, was panic-stricken. Well, I presume the /Minister of Railways and Canals was equally panic-stricken, he lost his head in the same way, because his own course was so thoroughly unjustifiable, so unbusinesslike and so unpatriotic, in sending to the States and paying larger prices. He said the price was a little larger, but he would not tell us what the price was exactly. What did this coal cost us ? He tells us that the coal cost $3.30 from the coal mines in Nova Scotia, and that the coal from the /States cost us somewhat more, but he won't give us the figures. He was bound to come here with detailed information when, as he tells us himself, he expected the most severe criticism.

The hon. gentleman, in comparing the Intercolonial Railway as respects coal supply writh the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, has failed to take account of the wide difference in the geographical situation. The Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway do not, at all events in this part of the Dominion, have the good fortune to have coal supplies on their railway lines. The Intercolonial Railway is in a favourable position, in that its line runs through coal fields in Nova Scotia and in Cape Breton ; so they can furnish

supplies from day to day, whereas in the case of the Grand Trunk Kailway and the Canadian Pacific Kailway it would be necessary to have a larger stock on hand. 1 do not say that as a reason why we should only have a two days' supply.
That would rather be a reason why you should have a supply on hand.

No, there is a good reason on the other hand why we should not stock up with coal. Coal deteriorates if it is piled up and exposed for a long time. But you get fresh coal from the Intercolonial Railway supplied frequently, instead of having a large quantity stored up. I quite agree that if you are going to have only one or two days' supply, it is running things too close ; but the experience last year was that, owing to various causes that my modesty prevents me from mentioning, the coal business was so active in Nova Scotia that every mine was pushed so that they could not keep up with orders for either government or private contracts. There was never a period in our history when the demand for coal was so great. And every private company found the same difficulty in having its contracts filled.
How did the strike come out ?

I think in the case of the Dominion Coal Company in Cape Breton they agreed to refer the matter to arbitration. The arbitration was recently completed, and I think the judgment was to the effect that owing to various circumstances that I need not enter Into, the wages were fair and reasonable, and so far as I know, the men did accept the judgment in good faith, and the work is now running smoothly.
I may mention that both in Cumberland and Pictou the demands of the men were granted.
I should say so, if the mines were pushed as the hon. gentleman says they were.

But the men had received considerable advantages, the men certainly received advantages in the general advance of trade.
Now, let me say to the hon. member for Lanark that we have reserved at his request, one general item which brings up the subject of the Intercolonial Railway, on which he desires to have a further discussion.
Department of the Secretary of State-Further amount required for clerical assistance, $400.

The Secretary of State has sent me a memorandum saying that this additional vote is necessary In consequence of $1,400 being accidentally
deducted from the total vote for contingencies in this department in the closing hours of last session, and in the rearrangement made necessary the department was $400 short.
Board of Civil Service Examiners-Further amount required, $250.
This is called for in consequence of an extra examination In the month of August, and by a large attendance for entrance in New Brunswick.

Will the Minister of Finance tell me why it is that items of this kind are so frequently found in the estimates ? Why are not things of this kind provided for in the main estimates? Why is it that there have to be so many items in the supplementary estimates every year ? It prevents us from getting a proper idea of the cost of each department. You have that divided up into three estimates. First you have the main estimate voted last year, then you have further supplementary estimates brought down near the end of the past session, then this session you have a third estimate, and sometimes a fourth and fifth. Now, could not some way be devised by which we can have the whole or a larger proportion of these in one main estimate?

I think it would be difficult. The hon. gentleman will find that this class of items in our supplementary estimates is not enlarged. In this class of estimates before us we are not dealing so much with things that are prospective, as with realities that have come before us. Take, for example, this little item. The information furnished is that it is owing to something that occurred in August, a special examination which had not been anticipated. The items in this respect are not unusual.
I am not saying they are.

I think the object of the hon. gentleman's question is quite right, and I agree with it.
Franchise Act-To cover over-expenditure upon printing the voters' lists tor last election, and to provide for printing any which may be required up to June 30, 1901, $10,000.

This is for printing. The printing of the voters' list last year cost $5.00(1 odd more than the vote, and the printing of the lists for byelections is estimated to cost $2,000, making the $7,000 which is required.

Will not the hon. minister give us what the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has asked for, the figure of the total expenditure ? We are asked for $10,000. Why can not the hon. gentleman scurry round and hunt up the other figures ?

The figures that I can give the hon. gentleman will only make $7,000, so that the item has to be reduced. The printing of the voters' lists last year cost .$5,000 odd more than the vote, and the printing of the list for byelections is estimated to cost $2,000, so that it is desired to provide $2,000 additional.
What was the vote in the first place ?
I cannot give the hon. gentleman that, I shall have to let the item stand and give the hon. gentleman that information later on.
We do not ask to have the item stand.

I will take note of the hon. gentleman's question.
To pay expenses in connection with the Chineses and Japanese Commission, $4,000.
This commission is now sitting and taking evidence. I have no hope that we can have the report for this session, but before many weeks are over the work of the commission will be completed.
The commission is sitting in British Columbia ?
Yes.
Who are the commissioners ?
Mr. Clute, Mr. Munn and Mr. Foley. Mr. Smith was a member of the commission.
Into what subject are they inquiring ?
Into the subject of Asiatic immigration, and the effect of it in British Columbia.
And Japanese immigration ?

Yes.
To recoup the North-west Mounted Police for relief to destitute half-breeds in the Northwest Territories, $500.
This Is the usual grant.
Yes.
If it Is the usual grant, why not put it into the main estimates ?
The mounted police for years past, have been authorized to afford relief to destitute Indians and half-breeds. This Is a small amount. Each year it amounts to perhaps $400 or $500.

I am not finding fault with the item. The only reason I have mentioned it is because it is a case Mr. WALLACE.
such as I have already spoken of to the hon. Minister of Finance. It seems to me that these items instead of being placed in the supplementary estimates should be in the main estimates.
No, we could not put this in the main estimates, because we did not know the amount. We received the yearly account after the main estimates were prepared, and we did not know what was required.
I think the hon. gentleman said it was the usual vote.
So it is.

Then, why do
you not put it in the main estimates ?

Because it may vary from year to year. It is sometimes more and sometimes less.
To pay J. Beatty amount of gratuity (revote), $187.33.

This is a little gratuity in the Customs Department which was voted last year, but owing to the fact that the amount lapsed, proceedings not having been taken to claim it, it has to be revoted.
Interest on amounts contributed to the superannuation fund by J. B. Ryan from December 31, 1896, to November 9, 1897, $8.17; and E. Kelly, from December 31, 1896, to November 9, 1897, $5.77, the date at which the contributions were repaid, $13.94.

This is an item to pay the balance of interest supposed to be due to some gentlemen in connection with superannuation money. I am advised it is an error and that the claim has already been discharged. Having given notice of the .fact, I presume they are satisfied as I have heard nothing to the contrary, and I am therefore, prepared to strike out the item. That disposes of this volume of estimates entirely.
Does that dispose of the supplementary estimates for the year 1900-1 ?

It clears up that particular volume, and it leaves in the main estimates one item in relation to the Intercolonial Railway which was allowed to stand in order that it might be made the basis of what is described as a full dress debate.
Mr. BORDEN ^Halifax). Then everything in the main estimates is disposed of with that exception ?

Yes; everything in the main estimates and in the first supplementaries for the current year. The supplementary estimtes for the coming year remain for consideration, and if the hon.

gentleman will turn to the militia estimates for the coming year, we will take these.
I would like to have one item reserved in the militia estimates on account of the absence of one of my hon. friend's.

Yes, all right.
Militia-Defences of Esquimau-Further sum required, $5,500.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE (Hon. F. W. Borden).
The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
This was found to be necessary.
* The money has been expended by the Dominion Rifle Association in connection with putting in telephone communication with the grounds and other improvements. I have satisfied myself that the expenditure is right, and this amount of money is necessary to make it good.
speakername: The FINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Has this been found necessary since the main estimates were brought down ?

Yes.
Military Properties-Further amount required, $29,700.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
This is also the result of a supple-plementary report from the engineer of my department, Mr. Weatherbee. This money is for some works that are in hand. I have the list of them here : New concrete floor, London, $250 ; repairs to drill hall, Port Hope, $2,500. Toronto, new Lot water system, Stanley barracks, $2,000 ; new floors, $250; porches and winter sashes, cavalry and infantry barracks, for saving fuel, $150; new range, cavalry barracks, $300. Montreal, fitting central room for 85tli Regiment in drill hall, $500 ; repairs Papineau road cemetery, $1,000 ; general repairs to Chambly fort, $1,000. Ottawa, new roof to drill shed, $3,500 ; changes in drill hall for four extra companies, bearer and engineer companies, additional accommodation, $2,000. Storm 167
porch, &c., for drill hall, Quebec, $350 ; additional accommodation in the Quebec cartridge factory, $1,200. Fredericton, repairs and alterations to plumbing, &e., $1,000. Annapolis, repairs to buildings at the old fort, $200. Winnipeg, new water supply, cavalry barracks, $500. New Westminster, installation of hot water system, $1,200.
To pay tor lauds expropriated for Work Point barracks, Esquimalt, $7,200.
The MINISTER OF MILITIA ANI) DEFENCE. This is in connection with the arrangement between the Canadian government and the British government, by which we undertook to expropriate certain lands for their use. The value of these lands was fixed by the courts.

speechtext: We pay for them in the first instance, and then we are reimbursed, I suppose.

Yes.
Monuments for Battlefields-Monument at Eccles' Hill, $400.
Mr. BRITTON, Is it the intention of the government to place tablets in the Royal Military College to the memory of the graduates who have been killed in battle, or lost their lives in the service of the empire ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
That has been mentioned by hon. gentlemen opposite, and I believe we will do it, but it can be taken out of contingencies and does not require a special vote.
Arms, ammunition, &c., $100,000.

The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I was going to suggest that.
Halifax provisional garrison, $338,000.

The committee understands why this expenditure is necessary. Over a year



ago the Canadian government, *with the approval of parliament, offered to release the battalion of infantry which was stationed at Halifax, until the war in South Africa is over. We have no information yet from the Imperial authorities as to when that battalion will return.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I saw it stated in the papers that it is the intention of the Imperial authorities to send a battalion of regulars to Halifax.
I think not. We have no official knowledge of it.

Yes.

There is nothing in the main estimates with regard to this. We did not include it in them because we did not know what news would be received about this, and we put it off until the last moment.
Geological Survey-To provide for additional plotting and compiling of surveys, plans, maps, and utilizing field notes, &c., $4,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Why was this not included in the main estimates V
Because my attention was not called to it by the acting director.

I think it is very desirable that the acting director should call the attention of the minister to it in time, so that it could be put in the main estimates. I have been suggesting to the Minister of Finance that it is desirable, as far as possible, to have all these items provided for in the main estimates, so that when we look at them we may see what a particular department requires.

I think the hon. gentleman's suggestion is a good one ; but, unfortunately, departmental officers have a very bad habit of making a general calculation for the main estimates very early in the year, and then having to provide for a few hundred dollars at the latter end of the year. I think the Indian Department is a special offender in that respect. My attention was called to the matter this session, and I think I shall be able to remedy it for the future.

I have been asked several times by correspondents to send them certain reports or information respecting the Geological Survey. I would like to ask the minister if the members of the House are supplied with the same number of copies of reports of the Geological Department as Mr. BORDEN (King's).
of the other departments of the government? Some small charges are made for copies of the reports. Is there a different rule applied to these reports than with regard to the reports of other departments, and if so, what is the reason ?

Yes, there is an order in council which has been in force for several years, providing that a certain scale of fees shall be paid for reports of the Geological Department. Whether it be a sound policy or not, I have not myself considered. I think, perhaps, the reason that policy was adopted in the first instance was that geological reports are of such a character that people who do not intend to make any special use of them are inclined to call for them. The result was that large numbers of these reports were constantly being called for through members of the House and members of the Senate, and were not being put to any real scientific use ; and it was thought that a small charge made to everybody would probably prevent that practice, and would avoid the expense of having to print a very large number.
What has been the effect of putting on that small charge ?
The effect has been that the reports are not required to be printed in very large numbers, and only those actually wanted for real use are called for.
Has the minister any idea of what revenue is derived from the sale of these reports ?
I have not. It is very small.

It appears to me that if the revenue is a mere bagatelle, it might be well to supply the members of the House with a number of copies of these reports. It seems to me that the dissemination among the people of the country of the information they contain would justify that course and the withdrawal of the fee. It is only a small matter, but it is vexatious. I would suggest that the minister should look into that.
I will consider it.

I wished to get a small report of the Geological Survey on the Nipis-sing district, and I had to pay 50 cents for it. It was a very small report, and its scarcity was given to me as the reason why I had to pay so much.
There is an order in council which specifies the prices of the reports.
I may say that this was one of the reports published before the plan was adopted of putting the price on the ' cover. I think the report was for 1869.

I would like to ask if the department supplies any publishing bouse with these reports ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
No.

Some years ago I applied to the department for one of these reports, and was referred to a publishing house in Toronto, and I had to pay 82 for it.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Will the hon. gentleman say how long ago that was ?

Five or six years ago, perhaps a little more.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
The minister then in charge of the department would probably be able to give the reason. I cannot see any reason, because all these reports are printed in the Printing Bureau, and are held by the librarian of the Survey, and are disposed of by him.
Does the hon. minister say that these reports cannot be bought at bookstores ? If I am not mistaken, I was referred there myself.

I do not say that at all, because it is quite competent for a man who keeps a bookstore to buy them and keep them for customers, and sell them either at cost or at a small advance. It may have been a report of which there was a small stock, and the librarian may have referred to some publishing house who he knew had it. They are not furnished to the publishing houses unless they pay for them.
Or to any book-store ?
No.
There is a misunderstanding about this.
I was speaking to the best of my knowledge.
I think the department furnishes these to the book-stores at a price, and the stores retail them to people who want them.

I find a very much greater demand for those publications now than there was eight or ten years ago. We are becoming a mining people. Young men are attending schools where the subjects dealt with in these reports are taken up, and I am quite sure that the hon. minister will find that if these reports were put on the market at a very moderate price-sufficient perhaps to cover the cost of paper and binding-there would be a very considerable sale for them. It would be wise to have a larger number printed. I fail to see why the government should not distribute publications of this kind to young people who 167}
are devoting their time to studying the subjects dealt with in these reports, and distribute them perhaps without any charge. I think it would be good policy to give each member eight or ten copies of a good many of these publications. I know that I could find a profitable distribution of them very readily to men who have taken up the subjects treated. Our usual plan, when parties write me for those publications, is to say that there is a certain charge for them and that they can be only procured from the department. If we want to distribute knowledge and assist young men to take up subjects of that kind, the free distribution would be a good thing. I would recommend the hon. minister to have a larger number printed because in years to come a very large number will be called for.

The remarks of the hon. gentleman are pretty much the same as those I made th# late director of the Survey some time ago. I think it would be very desirable that accurate information should be widely diffused with regard to our mining resources. While the Geological Survey has done very good work, the time has come when some little reorganization of the department is required. I have given some attention to the subject, and I hope to be able to suggest changes which will improve that branch of the service in the direction indicated. My idea is that the time has now arrived when some practical method should be adopted in carrying out the idea of the founder of the Survey, namely, to make M; the practical means of developing the country. I do not know that forcing the circulation of the reports would attain the end the hon. gentleman has in view. I think that a different kind of publication, devoted particularly to giving economic information with regard to the resources of the country, which could be brought within a very much smaller compass than the reports of the Geological Survey, would be more useful. The reports comprise detailed information with regard to every movement of every technical office in the field, but a very much smaller publication devoted to a practical statement of the economical results of the year's work, would be of very great value if properly circulated. The publication of such a statement, even considerably oftener than annually, would be most desirable. The hon. gentleman is aware that many men who are practical miners and prospectors, and who simply want a suggestion as to the places they should operate in, are men who cannot understand the reports of the Survey because they are not acquainted with the scientific terms and the technical manner of describing formations. Give that information in language which any ordinary person would readily understand, and you would have a very valuable publication.

Can these reports he had at the book-store? ?
The MINISTER OB1 THE INTERIOR. I think so.
To provide an additional amount for repairs to Caughnawaga mission-house, $1,700.

Has the hon. minister had any complaints from the Six Nation Indians on the Grand River reserve in the county of Brant, with regard to an alleged outbreak of smallpox and which, it is claimed, is nothing more than an allegation. Perhaps the hon. Minister of Customs has some knowledge of this. My attention has been called to the fact that no smallpox existed, but that the physician in charge, Dr. Secord, made the statement that the disease did exist. That was some time ago, and there is no proof of it. But, while smallpox does not exist on the reserve, by way of quarantine and other expenses the money of the Indians is being used up and they are protesting against this unnecessary and unwarranted expenditure. Has this matter been brought to the attention of the hon. minister and has he taken any action ?
The MINISTER OB'1 THE INTERIOR. It has not been brought to my attention. I did not hear of it until the hon. gentleman spoke. I know Dr. Secord. He is supposed to be a very competent medical officer, and I would have a good deal of confidence in anything he said. I will look up the case and see if there is any correspondence in the department in connection with it. Did the occurrence take place lately 9

The time is not stated, but I have a petition here signed by the Indians by way of protest against this expenditure and asking Mr. Macrae to examine and report to the department. The Indians say that there is no foundation for the statement that smallpox exists there. I will not take the responsibility of saying there is foundation for anything stated in this petition.
Will the hon. gentleman read the statement ?
I prefer not to.
The hon. gentleman might read some parts of it.
It would, perhaps, be unfair to Dr. Secord, if it were not true.
Is it signed by the chiefs ?

No, but one of the allegations is that a few of the chiefs, I believe eleven out of sixty, were brought together under some influences that were not stated, and took upon themselves to vote money as at an Indian council, which was illegal. I have handed the petition over to the Minister of the Interior, and I will ask him, before the House rises, to look into and give Mr. SIFTON.
us some information on the matter. I would not like to make any statement on the matter without being in possession of the facts. But if there is foundation for it, the statement in the petition should be inquired into.

The reserve is close to Brantford, and I have noticed in the Brantford papers statements that there was smallpox on the reserve and that a pretty strict quarantine had been established against it, I think, at Caledonia, Hamilton and Brantford. I believe that lately they have narrowed the circle, the people within which are not allowed to visit these places. I Should be much surprised if there were no cases there. Dr. Secord is well up in his profession, and he is not alone, for I believe there is an associate doctor there. I think also that he has been in consultation with Caledonia doctors. However, I do not wish to say anything about it until we have the facts. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) having this communication from the Indians, is quite right in bringing it up. I cannot see what object the medical officer could have had if there are no cases. Of course, he might be deceived. But he could hardly have any object in misrepresenting the case, because the statement that there was smallpox on the reserve would make necessary greater attention and the expenditure of more time on his part.

Of course, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) knows that in these smallpox cases there are strong differences of opinion as to whether the disease is really smallpox or not. We had experience of that in Edmonton two or three weeks ago. The local doctor said the disease which had broken out was not smallpox and refused to carry out the quarantine regulation. The result was that the smallpox spread, and we had to send more experienced men to enforce the quarantine. In so serious a matter as smallpox, the medical attendant on the reserve would not be justified in taking chances. I see that the petition is dated the 9th of the month. This is the first I have seen of it, but I will look into it.
Department of Indian Affairs-Ontario and Quebec-To provide an amount for legal expenses, $2,000.
Strike that out. That is inserted by mistake.
Had it been voted before ?

It was inserted by mistake by the Finance Department. It is not in my estimates properly.
Department of Indian Affairs-Manitoba and North-west Territories-To provide an amount for the purchase of live stock, Indian reserves, $13,000.
Are these cattle for breeding purposes ?
Yes, we have been providing cattle in this way for some years.
What class are they, just ordinary cattle ?

The plant was sold to Mr. Garrison, of Vir-den. I cannot remember the exact figure at present, I think it was something like $300. It was sold under the direction of the late Indian commissioner, and the records do not show that the money has ever been paid. I have given directions to my deputy to give instructions to have the money collected, if

The practice is to provide pure-bred sires- pedigreed animals. The heifers are generally grade.
it could be done.
Was it sold by the late Indian commissioner, Mr. Forget ?

There was a discussion some time ago about placing on the reserves Highland cattle or Galloways, or Polled Angus, to enable the Indians to make use of the knowledge they have in tanning the hides. I mention it to the minister so that he can think about it and, perhaps, at some time, give the Indians cattle that would enable them to develop a useful industry.

With a view of carrying out that idea I gave directions this year that a few Polled Angus should be put on where the breeding cattle were of the same. Of course, it is desirable not to cross them. The majority of the cattle there are Shorthorns, for that breed have proved the best.
What breed are they-just ordinary cattle ?

To some extent. We intend out of this vote to buy a couple of stallions. But it is an expensive matter to do much in the way of horse-breeding, and we have not so much confidence in it as a profitable industry for the Indians as we have in cattle-breeding. Cattle-breeding on the Indian reserves has been a pronounced success. Skilled buyers say that they get as good cattle from the Indian reserves as from anywhere else. This is due almost entirely to the practice inaugurated some years ago of sending pure-bred sires to the reserve. I think something can be done in the breeding of horses, but it must be gone into at first in a moderate way. The best way to proceed is by introducing a better class of sires, but we cannot go into that very largely on account of the expense involved in buying them and because they must be very carefully looked after.
Department of Indian Affairs-To provide an additional amount for day, boarding and industrial schools, Manitoba and the North-west Territories, $6,800.

In connection with this item, perhaps the hon. minister is in a position to-night to give us the explanation he promised with reference to the printing plant for the industrial school at Elkhorn. He stated he was not in possession of the full facts of the case, but he would bring it up on the supplementary estimates.
Yes.

The information I have is a little different from what I have been getting in reply to questions during the last two years. I brought this matter up three or four times, two years ago, and in the session of 1S99. I had heard all about this question, and I put four questions on the Order paper. I will give the committee the history of this case. At the time the late government decided to teach trades in the industrial school, the trade of printing was taken up, and a plant was established in the year 1S93, and a gentleman named Thompson was engaged as instructor. He also edited a weekly paper in that school. It was a non-political paper, it acquired a nice circulation, and was well patronized by the advertising community. It was conducted until 189S, when it was decided by this government to cease the teaching of these trades. Mr. Thompson having entered into these arrangements with the business people, having received subscriptions in advance, was desirous of continuing the publication of the paper. He visited the city of Winnipeg and met the Indian commissioner, Mr. Forget. As a result of that visit, he leased the plant from the Indian commissioner, on a stipulation that if either party were desirous of annulling the contract he could do so by giving six months' notice. But Mr. Thompson was assured by Mr. Forget that no doubt the plant would be left with him until such time as the government might again take up the teaching of printing. He was. therefore, greatly surprised to find that, inside of two months after he had leased it, a six months' notice was served upon him. He could not understand it. He asked for an explanation from the Indian commissioner, who stated that he could not give any information other than that it was done upon the authority of the Minister of the Interior. Mr. Thompson heard that it was being handed over to Mr. Garrison, the gentleman named by the Minister of the Interior, who was the editor of a Liberal paper in the town of Virden, and seeing it was the intention to crowd it out of that town, he decided, before the six months was up, to purchase a plant of his own, and to continue the publication of a paper, which he did, setting aside the government plant. Mr. Gar-

rison took tlie plant into Ills possession. Now, as I was aware of these facts, two years ago I asked the Minister of the Interior what had become of this plant, if it had been leased or sold. The reply was that it had not been leased, it had not been sold, but it was in possesion of Mr. Garrison, and that negotiations for its sale were then pending. Well, I allowed one year to pass by, and last session I repeated the question, asking in addition if the government was aware that this plant was being utilized for the publication of a Liberal paper in the constituency of Brandon, represented by the Minister of the Interior, a paper called the Griswold Ledger. The reply to that was given by the acting minister, that the government had not leased it, even then, last year. That was long after the Indian commissioner had stepped out. They had not sold it, and they were not aware it was utilized for publication by another paper. I brought this fact to his attention, and I told him that this plant had been sold to Mr. Wildman, who was publishing the Griswold Ledger. I made so strong a case that the acting minister promised to have an investigation. I repeated my question here when the main estimates were up, and the Minister of the Interior told me that it had been sold to Mr. Garrison. He tells me to-night that it has been sold under the Indian commissioner, Mr. Forget, and that he has not received the money, though Mr. Garrison has sold it and obtained the money himself for it. It seems very strange that a plant that the late government, I understand, paid about $800 for, and placed in this school for teaching the trade of printing to the pupils and for the printing of a weekly paper, should be handed over to a political friend and not a single dollar obtained for the same, allowing that political friend to dispose of it to another political friend who has paid for the plant. Now, I am informed that Mr. Wildman, who is now the editor of the paper published on this plant, had heard that Mr. Garrison had no right to sell the plant, and some time ago communicated writh the department, and the Information he received from Ottawa was that it was all right, that Mr. Garrison had authority to dispose of the plant. At any rate, by the minister's own words to-night, the government sold the plant to Mr. Garrison. though it looks to me as if it had been a gift to him. Certainly, he has not paid a dollar for it, though Mr. Garrison himself has disposed of the plant and has been paid for it by Mr. AVildman, and it has been used these last two years for publishing a Liberal paper in the town of Griswold ; and still the department, one year ago, knew nothing about it. I think this case demands further investigation by the minister, in order to harmonize these different views of the acting minister and himself. The Indian commissioner certainly placed the whole responsibility upon the Minister of the Interior, Mr. ROCHE.
for he stated that it was upon the authority of the Minister of the Interior that this lease was cancelled. Now, if the government wished to dispose of the plant they could have done so to Mr. Thompson, who would have purchased it and paid for it. It seems, however, that Mr. Thompson would not publish a political paper, supporting the government, on that plant, and, therefore, it was taken out of his possession. I do not think that is the way in which the property of the country should be disposed of, and some further explanation is required.

I have had from the start no actual knowledge with regard to the transaction, and was not aware of what was done until after it was done. AVhen the hon. gentleman asked the question two years ago, the answer was given from the records of the department, so far as they show. AVhen the hon. gentleman raised this question some time ago, I communicated with the officers of my department, asking for a reply, and this is the answer :
This plant was leased to Mr. Thompson, formerly printing instructor at the school, free of charge in consideration of the continuation of the printing shop connected with the school, determinable upon six months' notice, which was given and the plant transferred to Mr. Garrison, of Virden. There is nothing on file to show the ultimate disposal of the plant, and our books do not eontaiu any entry of moneys received for the sale. If any further transfer took place It must have been arranged by the Indian Commissioner, who was instructed that the plant might be sold to Mr. Garrison at a valuation to be made by a competent valuator, If he considered It necessary.
The only point in connection with this is that Air. Garrison has not paid for the plant.
Some resolutions reported.

It is now near midnight, and as to-morrow is a religions holiday, we do not want to work after twelve o'clock. I move, therefore, that the committee rise and report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-VISIT OF THE DUKE OF YORK.

speechtext: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir AArilfrid Laurier) moved the adjournment of the House.

subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-VISIT OF THE DUKE OF YORK.
speechtext:
Air. Speaker, before the House adjourns, I would like to call the attention of the right hon. Prime Alinister to a letter I received from Halifax this morning, in regard to the visit of their Royal Highnesses the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall. It is as follows :

R.	L. Borden, Esq., M.P.,
Ottawa.
Mayor's Office,
Halifax, N.S., May 11, 1901.
Dear Sir,-There is a rumour here that the government might require their Royal Highnesses the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall and York, when visiting Canada, to make their landing at some port other than Halifax.
The city council have, by resolution, requested me to write to you and explain that any change from the published programme of landing at Halifax when visiting Canada would not meet with the approval of the citizens of Halifax, as we have made an appropriation and are making arrangements for the reception; and hope to have the presence and assistance of representatives of both Dominion and local governments.
Yours truly,

Mayor.
I understand that the right hon. gentleman gave an answer in regard to this same question to an hon. gentleman this morning, hut as the letter has come since, and the matter is more or less urgent, I take the opportunity of bringing it to the attention of the government, in order that they may have before them the views of the mayor and corporation of the city of Halifax. I know it will be a very great disappointment to the people of Halifax generally if the arrangement which they thought was provided for should not be carried out.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W.
S.	Fielding). I may say that I have also had communications of the same nature, but a moment's reflection will show my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) that the arrangements of this kind, especially at the beginning, must of necessity be more under the control of the Imperial authorities than under the control of the Canadian government. We may have something to do with the arrangements later on. but in the initiation of the arrangements, we must rely very largely on the judgment of the authorities at home.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12 o'clock-midnight.
Feiday, May 17, 1901.
